articles.headline: What is going on with Kristaps Porzingis and his Warriors absence?
keyFacts: Golden State Warriors veteran Kristaps Porziņģis has not played this season due to health issues and stepped away before training camp.
The Warriors are withholding Porziņģis' salary payments because he is not rendering services, and sources report he is leaning toward retirement.
The Warriors front office is pursuing trade options utilizing Porziņģis' contract and may wait until February before making further decisions.
body: Golden State Warriors veteran Kristaps Porziņģis has not played this season, and based on recent reporting, he may not play again any time soon.

Porziņģis, who is battling health issues, stepped away from the organization before training camp began even though he still has two seasons remaining on his contract. As such, the organization is withdrawing payment because he is not rendering services in his contract. He is officially listed as "not with team" rather than as having a "general illness" as previously described.
Golden State head coach Steve Kerr said the Warriors were " caught off guard " by the decision by Porziņģis. The team is reportedly " pessimistic " that he will ever play for them again.
Here is more from ESPN :

"The Golden State Warriors are not delivering semimonthly payments to veteran center Kristaps Porzingis on his $20 million salary, league sources told ESPN, ruling that the currently absent center is not rendering his services. General manager Mike Dunleavy and the Warriors' front office are still actively pursuing trade avenues utilizing Porzingis' contract even as the 31-year-old leans toward ending his NBA career."
It is notable, of course, that Porziņģis is reportedly not receiving his contract and is leaning towards ending his career.

Porziņģis is reportedly not challenging the decision by Golden State, even if it is costly. According to The Athletic , the NBPA is currently " aligned " with the stance to not challenge the Warriors. But they don't agree on everything.
Here is more :

"[The] organization and Porziņģis’ camp still appear to disagree behind the scenes about what, exactly, is keeping the 31-year-old off the floor. Dunleavy and Kerr have publicly cited only a health issue, while Porziņģis’ continued absence has fueled speculation that he may retire from the sport."
The big man shared his perspective with regard to his absence on social media in mid-October.

Golden State does not currently have plans to permanently void his contract. If it were to happen, though, it is unlikely to happen until February so that Golden State's front office can first survey the trade market before the deadline.
Potential trade suitors could have interest in Porziņģis because they could get rid of an unwanted long-term salary or fetch an additional draft pick compensation in return.

Until then, the situation remains messy between the 2024 NBA champion and the Warriors. But as both sides wait for a resolution with regard to his health, which matters most, there is no clear right answer.
This article originally appeared on For The Win: What is going on with Kristaps Porzingis and his Warriors absence?

articles.headline: Aaron Pico eager to rematch Lerone Murphy: 'I know I can beat him'
keyFacts: Aaron Pico said he wants a rematch against Lerone Murphy, who knocked him out in his UFC debut.
Pico stated that a rematch with top-ranked Murphy would bring him closer to fighting for a title.
Pico also expressed interest in fighting Movsar Evloev in the future, though he expects Evloev to return later.
body: Aaron Pico wants to right his wrong against Lerone Murphy.

Pico (15-5 MMA, 2-1 UFC) was knocked out by Murphy in his octagon debut at UFC 319 . He has since rebounded with back-to-back wins over Patricio Freire and a first-round knockout of Losene Keita at UFC 333 . As Pico looks to continue his ascent up the featherweight ladder, he sees a rematch vs. Murphy (17-1-1 MMA, 9-1-1 UFC) making sense.
He thinks he was merely caught when they first fought.

"I want that fight," Pico told MMA Junkie of Murphy. "And people are going to ask me, 'Why do you want that fight?' I'm a competitor. I want to fight and get that one back. I mean, obviously you watch the fight, I was beating him up. If I just would have been a little bit smarter, I would have gotten that win.

"But there's a lot of lessons that came because of the loss, and that's the reason that I would love to run it back. And why wouldn't I? He's top five in the world, so it just puts me closer to fighting for a title, and I know I can beat him. So yeah, I would love to fight him for sure."

Another fighter Pico is targeting is Movsar Evloev (20-1 MMA, 10-1 UFC), whom he was scheduled to debut against before Evloev withdrew. Evloev was finished by featherweight champion Alexander Volkanovski at UFC 333 , which makes him a realistic matchup for Pico – but maybe not quite yet.

"I'd love to fight Movsar," Pico said. "We were supposed to fight, but I think it's going to be a while before he comes back. I mean, especially after that and his long training camp. Stylistically, that's a really good matchup for me, but I don't know when he's going to return. I don’t think it's going to be anytime soon."
This article originally appeared on MMA Junkie: Aaron Pico eager to rematch Lerone Murphy: 'I know I can beat him'

articles.headline: More than a thumping, possibly a realignment
keyFacts: Democrats won majorities in both the Senate and the House, reversing Republican 2024 victories across seven key target states.
The author attributed Republican losses to Donald Trump's tariffs, candidate choices, and conduct that alienated key voter demographics.
Long-term political realignment remains uncertain and will depend on future policy decisions, economic trends, and voter reactions.
body: More than a “thumping.” That’s what George W. Bush called it when Democrats won majorities in both houses by gaining 6 Senate and 30 House seats in 2006. As this is written, before sunrise Wednesday, Democrats have won majorities in both houses, gaining seven Senate seats, with chances at two more, and have gained or are ahead in 40 Republican House seats.
Quite a reversal from 2024. As Republican pollster Patrick Ruffini notes , Trump’s party may end up holding no House seat that voted for President Donald Trump by less than 9 points two years ago.

Trump likes to boast that he carried all seven target states in his 50% to 48% popular-vote reelection. This year, all seven — Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, North Carolina, Pennsylvania, Wisconsin — went Democratic.

Much, maybe nearly all of this is Trump’s doing. His “Liberation Day” tariffs, and the frivolous way he kept adjusting tariffs up and down, clearly kept inflation up and produced no visible positive effect. Like Joe Biden’s belief in Democrats’ historic remedy of pump-priming spending, Trump’s idiosyncratic belief in the power of tariffs proved destructive for his standing and his party’s.

Trump’s insistence on slavish loyalty in selecting candidates has also cost Republicans dearly. His choices in Georgia (2021 and 2022) and Arizona (2020 and 2024), his failure to get candidates who lost by less than 1 percentage point across the finish line in Wisconsin and Michigan in 2024, and his picks this year in North Carolina, South Carolina, and Texas have arguably cost the party nine Senate seats heading into 2027.

That’s the difference between a Democratic Senate with 54 or 55 seats and a Republican Senate with the same majority. Between a Senate that confirms Republican Supreme Court nominees and one that invokes the Mitch McConnell precedent to refuse even to consider them. Between a Senate that might seriously consider convicting and removing an impeached president and one that would reject the effort outright.

As always, small numbers can make big differences in a 100-member Senate. Odds tend to prevail in elections for all 435 House members. And overall, the numbers in the public polls have held up pretty well this year, as pollsters have been making reasonable adjustments to lower response rates from Republicans — a subject on which I may comment later, and many others will soon.
And the messages from comparisons between the 2026 exit poll and 2024 exit poll stack up pretty well with the county election reports pouring in over the last 24 hours.

Republican percentages this year seem to be about 6 percentage points lower than Trump’s 2024 percentages among the most-watched demographic groups — whites, men and women, white college graduates and non-graduates, and various income groups.

In the county returns, we see central-city counties post overwhelming Democratic percentages, suggesting a sweep of almost every precinct. We see Republican majorities in suburban and exurban counties atrophying in the Southeast and disappearing in Texas. We see Republican percentages holding up only in the most un-metropolitan rural counties.

We see some interesting regional patterns. In far northern states, Republican candidates for senator and governor did not lag as far behind Trump’s 2024 levels, perhaps for local reasons: Sen. Susan Collins’s (R-ME) personal popularity, Democratic scandals in Minnesota, and Abdul el Sayed’s divisiveness in Michigan kept Democrats from running more than 1, 3, and 4 points ahead of Kamala Harris.

In contrast, Democratic Senate candidates ran 11 points ahead of Harris in North Carolina, South Carolina and Georgia and 7 points ahead in Florida. We see here that the slow and steady movement of Northeasterners down I-95 and I-85 over the years has made the South Atlantic states, at least this year, the scene of close partisan battles, just as the once-Republican states in the Northeast became in the wake of the New Deal three generations ago. The biggest surprise was the Democratic victories in South Carolina, which had the nation’s fastest percentage population growth in 2025 to 2026.

Note also that nationally, there were significant Republican declines, by double digits, among Hispanics, Asians and “others”—groups among which Trump posted gains in 2024. Hispanics and Asians voted about 27% Republican in 2012 and 2016 , 46% and 40% Republican, respectively, in 2024, and 35% and 29%, respectively, in 2026. Similarly, voters aged 18 to 29 showed increasing support for Trump in 2024 and sharply reduced levels in 2026.

This decline in Republican support wreaked havoc with the party’s efforts, urged on by Trump, to draw new congressional district lines in Republican-controlled states. These inspired similar efforts by Democrats, which in California proved successful, while declining Republican percentages among Hispanics produced “dummymanders” that backfired, especially in Texas and North Carolina. In the latter, House Republican campaign committee chairman Rep. Richard Hudson (R-NC) lost his seat—the first such loss I can recall since House Democratic campaign chairman James Corman lost in the San Fernando Valley in 1980.

Will those 2024 gains turn out to be a one-time phenomenon? Or do they remain harbingers of a possible future? No one knows for sure, and voters themselves are poor prognosticators of their own future attitudes. But I suspect the big drop among these volatile groups—Hispanics and Asians tend to be younger than average—can be explained by a sense that the second-term Trump hasn’t lived up to his basic campaign promise.

His most effective 2024 ad, as I wrote three weeks ago, showed video of Kamala Harris emphasizing her support for government-paid surgery for transgender prison inmates, with the tagline, “Kamala is for they/them, President Trump is for you.” He underlined that message visually by working a McDonald’s fry station and a drive-through window in the target state of Pennsylvania.

Trump’s conduct since November 2024 has undermined his “cares about people like me” message. Tariffs and military action against Iran and in the Gulf of Hormuz suggested an indifference to the inflationary pain they seemed to cause ordinary people. The new White House ballroom, the triumphal arch (with military uses) and his threat to demolish the Kennedy Center unless his name was put on it suggested a preoccupation with celebrating himself that was capped by his election-eve address at the Reflecting Pool, inviting comparison with the mythical Narcissus who couldn’t stop looking at his own reflection.

These are personal flaws, but they damaged a party he has battered into subservience. They benefited an opposition party that most voters, polls show, view negatively and expect little from — and whose hold on twentysomethings, Hispanics, Asians and other more volatile voting groups remains uncertain.

This year’s vote is an attempt to put limits on the actions and vagaries of a disappointing incumbent president. It is not atypical of our era of polarized political parity, in which, in seven of the last nine presidential elections, voters have given the winner’s party trifectas — control of the presidency, Senate and House — and in six of those seven cases have withdrawn the trifecta in the off-year election two years later.

Are we looking at the beginning of a political realignment? Toward some period of Democratic dominance rather than the two-party parity we’ve enjoyed (or endured) since 1994? RealClearPolitics analyst Sean Trende, author of what I consider the best book on the 1952-92 alignment, The Lost Majority , tweeted on election night, “Just understand that you’re seeing something special, a 100-year flood. Easily the worst election for a party since 1974.”

I’m not so sure. It could turn out to be, but that depends on political decisions that have not yet been made and exogenous events (macroeconomic trends, technological advance, wars) that have not yet occurred. This year’s results sit just at the outer limits of the two-party parity we have enjoyed (or endured) since the presidential election of 1992 and the congressional elections of 1994.

Democrats have dominated the presidency, narrowly, winning four of seven elections, with an average popular vote margin of 49 to 46 percent. That’s significantly narrower than Republicans’ 52 to 45 percent average popular vote margin in the ten elections from 1952 to 1988. In seven of those ten elections, one party won more than 53 percent of the popular vote. Since then, no one has; Barack Obama came closest with 52.9 percent in 2008.

The 1992 election that brought Bill Clinton to the White House also gave Democrats their 40th year in control of the House of Representatives by a 258 to 176 margin. Democrats had won at least 243 seats in every election since 1958. Neither party has won 258 House seats since, and only twice in 30 years has either party (Democrats in 2008, Republicans in 2014) won more than 243. Democrats this year are topping 243 but will not reach 257, as they did in 2008, or top the 258 that for decades was the party’s norm.

In the 16 Senate elections starting in 1994, Republicans have ended up with majorities in 10 and Democrats in 6, with the votes split almost evenly. Only once, and for only eight months, did either party have a 60-vote filibuster-proof majority: Democrats from July 2009, when Al Franken was sworn in as winner of the contested Minnesota race, until February 2010, when Scott Brown was sworn in after winning the special election to replace Edward Kennedy.

Other than during that Congress, neither party has emerged from an election with more than 55 seats, a level Republicans reached in 1996 and 1998 and Democrats reached in 2012 and will reach again if, as is unclear at this writing, they win either of the seats up this year in Alaska and Mississippi, and will exceed if they win both.

Democrats’ House and Senate margins this week look impressive by the standards of 1994-2026, though ordinary by those of 1952-90. Do they signal the start of an extended period of political dominance, like the 36 years Republicans enjoyed after their landslide in 1894? That election overturned the 218-124 Democratic majority elected two years earlier and produced a 253-93 Republican supermajority. History offers some perspective.

Start with the two Democratic gains of 2006 and 2008, which left them, after some litigation and until a special election defeat, with a supermajority in the Senate and a 250-plus Democratic House like the one they just won. Despite the failure of the Clintons’ health care plans with similar majorities, Barack Obama decided to go with major health insurance reform and, when Democrats lost their 60th Senate seat, Speaker Nancy Pelosi plunged ahead.

The problem was, and is, that most Americans have health care plans they like. That’s why Obamacare tested negatively when Obama was in office and Obamacare repeal tested negatively when Donald Trump and Republicans threatened to repeal it. Many Democrats, notably the leftists calling for Medicare for All, want government-provided health care. It’s likely voters won’t.

The question is whether Democrats in 2027-28 can come up with policies they can enact in 2029 that won’t be rejected by voters in 2030. And by 2030, they may be facing a decision on what to do when current law requires cutting Social Security benefits. Progressives may want to cut affluent recipients’ benefits or increase taxes on those earning above $184,500, but affluent suburbanites who are now a dominant constituency in the party may not like that.

Or consider the response of Democrats after the party won 61-37 and 291-144 majorities in the Watergate year of 1974 and held them as Jimmy Carter was elected president in 1976. This was a more ideologically diverse Democratic Party than today’s, with many Southern conservatives hostile to liberal policies. Dovish Democrats did cut off funding for South Vietnam in 1975, but went along as Carter increased defense spending in response to the Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979.

In an inflationary decade, the Democratic Congress cut capital gains taxes in 1978 and authorized 401(k) plans that later pushed out private-sector defined-benefit pensions. And led by Edward Kennedy, Ralph Nader and Carter appointee Alfred Kahn, the Democratic Congress deregulated trucking, airlines and freight rail. Under the adroit leadership of Tip O’Neill, Jim Wright and Tony Coelho, Democrats maintained House control for another dozen years, until Newt Gingrich prevailed in 1994, but were unable to prevent Republican presidential candidates from carrying 133 out of a possible 150 states in the elections of the 1980s.

Or consider the precedent of the Republican landslide of 1946, just after World War II. What Harry Truman called a “do-nothing Congress” actually did a lot, trimming back labor unions’ power in the Taft-Hartley Act, passed over Truman’s veto with Southern Democratic support, cutting tax rates sharply, and rejecting government as the prime provider of housing. On foreign policy, Republicans, led by Sen. Arthur Vandenberg, provided key support for Truman’s anti-communist policies.

But the Republicans were perhaps too successful. Taft-Hartley has lasted 79 years, and few politicians still advocate building more public housing. The Republican majorities, having done their work, were dismissed in 1948, and the party won a House majority only once in the next 46 years. Republicans did become successful, arguably dominant, at the presidential level when the G.I. generation expanded the electorate in 1952, but its thrust was to ratify rather than repeal the New Deal, albeit with 1947 modifications.

The really successful realignment year, in policy and politics, was 1894. Its enormous Republican gains were followed in 1896 by, in the title of Karl Rove’s biography , the triumph of William McKinley. Republicans won seven of the next nine presidential elections, with a popular vote average margin of 50 to 41 percent, and won majorities in Congress for 28 of 36 years.
WHAT’S AHEAD IF THE POLLS ARE RIGHT OR WRONG

But looking back, it seems that many propitious developments that fostered contentment with the governing party were the products of the private sector: mass industrialization resulting from technological advance, an industrial labor force supplied by open immigration from Europe in a country still so riven by the Civil War that there was minimal migration from the impoverished South to the growing North, the discovery of gold in the Yukon and Transvaal, stabilizing what had been deflationary currencies, the stabilization of the private sector through mergers and of banking by the creation of the Federal Reserve.

So elections which seem to trigger at least temporary political realignment can shape public policy and improve people’s lives. But not inevitably, and often not in ways intended or predicted. The 2026 election may be the harbinger of a political realignment, of a South as partisanly contested as the nation’s northern tier and of competition for the offspring of immigrants. Or it may just be another chapter in multiple decades of close competition in a politics of polarized parity, with a different cast of characters.

articles.headline: All Guardian Boss Lairs and rewards in The Division 2 Echoes of Central Park
keyFacts: The Echoes of Central Park DLC for The Division 2 introduces five Guardian bosses located across the new map after the campaign.
Destructoid reports that these five bosses were formerly SHD Agents transformed into monstrosities who possess unique signature skills and abilities.
Players can obtain exclusive skill variants and Apex Protocol gear pieces by defeating the Guardian bosses.
body: The Echoes of Central Park DLC has modified the endgame experience of The Division 2 with introduction of the Guardian bosses. Once you’re done with the campaign, you’ll find the mention of five bosses who are located all around the new map.

Once you reach the conclusion of the main story of Central Park, you’ll get to learn more about the Guardians. All five of them used to be SHD Agents, but consumption of something nefarious turned them into monstrosities.

The table below has information abut all the Signature Skills and abilities of all five Guardians.

Multithrow: Throws 3 foam grenades in quick succession. Mire Corrosive Trap Devour: Any triggered trap buffs Mire’s damage by 500% for 15 seconds.
Resilience: High health, low armor. Specter Blackout Seeker Predator’s Mark: Blinded players take 8% damage when they move.
Death Grip: When within 15 meters of his targets, Specter deals 500% more damage. Thorn Trophy System Enrage: Blinded players take 8% damage when they move
Lethal: When within 15 meters of his targets, Specter deals 500% more damage. Vulture Gas Chamber Grounded: Poisoned targets cannot sprint.
Dead Drop: When 15 meters away from his target, Vulture’s damage increases by 300%. All Guardian drops in The Division 2
The Echoes of Central Park DLC offers exclusive skills that will drop when you defeat these Guardians. There are six new variants to obtain by defeating them.
Howl (pulse variant): Main quest
Leech Hive (hive variant): Hollow
Gas Bomber (drone variant): Variant
Trophy System (drone variant): Thorn
Blackout Seeker (seeker mine variant): Specter
Corrosive Trap (trap variant): Mine
Additionally, you can also get the new Apex Protocol gear pieces. The pieces drop randomly, so you’ll have to kill the Guardians a fair number of times to complete the full set.
2+ pieces : +10% Weapon Damage, +10% Skill Damage
3+ pieces : +15% Weapon Handling, +15% Hazard Protection
4+ pieces : Apex Engine
Veer Failsafe (backpack talent): Receive +5% armor on kill and +10% skill damage per Apex Engine bonus stack.
Veer Override (chest talent): While at maximum Apex Engine stacks, enemies damaged by your Skills are marked for 10s. Deal +20% Amplified Damage to marked enemies.

articles.headline: Fenerbahce v Liverpool: Champions League – live
keyFacts: Fenerbahce took the lead against Liverpool when substitute Muriqi scored a header past goalkeeper Alisson.
Karen Carney said Liverpool appeared very flat-footed and questioned if their previous performance or fatigue was too much.
Alexander Isak scored a header for Liverpool shortly after coming off the bench following an assist from Gakpo.
body: “Some of it was like, ‘Have they ever played together before?’” says Karen Carney. “They were very flat-footed. I don’t know if the Arsenal performance, it was too much, the fatigue. I don’t think Fenerbahce were all that.”

90+3 mins: The ball doesn’t reach the keeper, and he scurries back in time to get on the ball and swing it into the area from just inside the Fenerbahce half. When it dips Gakpo taps back to Van Dijk, whose isn’t standing anywhere near the kind of spot from which he might score with a left-foot shot, and duly doesn’t score with his left-foot shot. And that is most likely that..

90+1 mins: Wide! Alisson comes out to deal with a long clearance, but his header towards Kerkez is intercepted by Guendouzi, and though the keeper reaches his pass first he sends it back to the former Arsenal midfielder, who shoots first-time from tight on the byline, about 60 yards out, but misses.
87 mins: Boos and whistles as Liverpool have the ball. They appear to be playing with a front four, with the substitute Koumas joining Gakpo, Isak and Barcola.
85 mins: Mac Allister is booked for bringing down Akturkoglu, and Fenerbahce have a decent chance to shoot from the resulting free-kick, which Akturkoglu himself appears to fancy.
84 mins: The commentator wonders what this result could do for Kuyt, “right at the start of his time as manager of Fenerbahce”. Um, I think you’ll find it’s the end.
81 mins: Ally McCoist on co-commentary wants to know why Alisson didn’t come for the cross as it arced slowly into the area, and really he is the one who might have prevented the goal.

And now Liverpool trail! It’s just an excellently-placed header from Muriqi, from eight yards or so. Brown’s cross from the right was the opposite of flat, and looped droopily onto the substitute’s head, but he planted it beyond Alisson’s reach and into the corner!
76 mins: More substitutions: Kahveci and Semedo go off for Fenerbahce, and Muldur and Akturkoglu come on. Meanwhile in like-for-like news Liverpool bring Kerkez on for Tsimikas.

75 mins: It’s a Kante cross chipped in from outside the area. Alisson comes for it but Gakpo, in front of him, gets his eyebrows to the ball and flicks it past his goalkeeper, leaving Brown with a tap-in!

71 mins: Nearly a lovely break from Liverpool let by Barcola, who eventually plays in Gakpo but the pass is fractionally overhit, the Dutchman decides that Ederson is going to get there first, and instead the ball rolls out of play.

Alexander Isak, seconds after coming off the bench, is presented with the best chance of the game by Gakpo’s left-wing cross, and though Ederson gets two hands to his header it’s from only three yards out and he can’t keep it out!
66 mins:Liverpool make a triple substitution: Gomes, Munoz and Ngumoha come off, Wirtz, Isak and Gakpo come on, and Barcola is shunted over to the right flank.
65 mins: Another save! It’s Muriqi, the freshly-arrived substitute, from away to the right of goal, with a shot that’s well struck but from too wide to beat Alisson.

61 mins: Gomez gets the ball in the Fenerbahce half and nobody closes him down, so he runs towards the penalty area, and then a bit further towards it, and at some point he decides he should probably have a shot now he’s this close, which inevitably he scuffs well wide.
59 mins: Munoz covers Brown’s run well enough, but he hits his clearance into the Fenerbace left-back’s chest and the rebound falls kindly for Brown to hammer a shot at goal, which is saved.

57 mins: Saved! And again saved! The first is Barcola’s shot towards the near post but turned around it, and the second is Van Dijk’s header from the resulting corner, which he should probably have buried but goes straight into Ederson’s gloves.

56 mins:Fenerbahce boot the ball out of defence pretty aimlessly, but when you’ve got Lukaku around these things can be useful, and he heads it on to Kahveci who’s suddenly scurrying into Liverpool’s half. But Nyoni does well to track him, and dispossess.

55 mins: Another better spell for Liverpool, though it would be a stretch to describe anything about this game as control. “Wondering about a Greek yoghurt conglomerate sponsoring a Turkish team,” wonders Tim Smith. “Would not appear to be the most natural of fits.” The (yoghurt) culture wars.
49 mins: The second half is continuing in much the same pell-mell vein as the first. Ngumoha goes on a nice run, which ends with a shot from a very acute angle, deflected wide for a corner.

It was a half of two halves for Liverpool, one encouraging, the other concerning, as the out-of-form sixth-best side in Turkey made them really uncomfortable. It wasn’t just the atmosphere they were struggling with. Still, they have parity, and their nominal striker – Barcola in the first half – can’t be any less influential in half two.
45+2 mins: A breathless half ends with an offside call against Barcola, but with the home side having enjoyed an excellent spell, and the scores level.
43 mins: Lukaku beautifully sets up a teammate for a shooting chance at the edge of the D. Sadly the player he sets up is Kante, who isn’t much of a goalscorer.

39 mins:Fenerbahce are really troubling Liverpool at the moment. They zip the ball around the edge of the visitors’ box for a while before working it to Greenwood, whose shot goes just wide of the near post.
35 mins: This is all very frantic. Iraola spoke yesterday about how his team needed “to try to kill the confidence and momentum they can have with the supporters”. They have not done that.
32 mins: Another chance for the Turks! This time Lukaku gets into the right side of the area but what follows is neither cross nor shot, and duly is a goal kick.

31 mins: It was not good defending from Jacquet, who jumped in the wall as if his priority was not preventing a goal but preventing himself getting hit, twisting to get himself side-on. The ball then skidded off his thigh, and past Alisson.

articles.headline: Hakeem Jeffries promises ‘affordability’ focus after Democratic midterm win
keyFacts: Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries celebrated Democrats winning control of both Congress chambers in the United States midterm elections.
Jeffries, set to become the first Black Speaker of the House, promised Democrats will focus on making life more affordable for everyday Americans.
Jeffries stated Democrats will take office in January and work to hold the Trump administration accountable while attempting to pass new laws.
body: Democratic House leader Hakeem Jeffries has celebrated his party’s sweeping victory in the United States midterm elections, calling the results an “American tsunami” as Democrats have taken control of both chambers of Congress.
“It wasn’t simply a blue wave. It was an American tsunami,” Jeffries said at a news conference on Wednesday, a day after Democrats pulled off upsets in several Republican strongholds.
Jeffries said Democrats expect to win at least 255 House seats once all vote counts are final, giving the party what he described as a historic majority.
“The American people have chosen common sense over corruption, chaos and cruelty,” he said.
Jeffries, who is set to become the first Black Speaker of the House when the new Congress takes office in January, said the results showed Americans wanted a change in direction.
“We’re humbled by the outcome,” he said, promising a “relentless effort to make life more affordable for everyday Americans”.
Speaking earlier on MS Now’s Morning Joe, Jeffries said Democrats would focus on getting things done rather than seeking revenge against President Donald Trump and his allies.
“We ran on affordability. We won on affordability. And now it’s our job to govern on affordability,” he said.

Democrats campaigned on bringing down the rising costs of groceries, petrol, housing and healthcare, which have left Americans feeling increasingly squeezed. But with Trump’s threats to use his presidential veto to block legislation he’s opposed to, Democrats may struggle to push through new laws even with a majority in Congress.

Jeffries pointed to a bipartisan housing affordability bill passed in July as an example of the types of legislation Democrats could pursue. The bill became law without Trump’s signature after he dismissed it as “a yawn” and “so unimportant”.
Jeffries also said Democrats would work to hold the Trump administration accountable for any wrongdoing, even as he acknowledged Americans wanted them to get things done, not “get even”.
“There’s a cost to corruption,” he said, adding that Democrats would follow the facts and the law, and “let the chips fall where they may”.

articles.headline: Trump says he’s not sure if Vance will run for president in 2028
keyFacts: President Donald Trump stated that he does not know for sure whether Vice President JD Vance will run for president in 2028.
Vice President JD Vance blamed the administration's unpopular Iran war for Republican losses in the midterm elections.
President Donald Trump defended the Iran war and stated he would not have done anything differently.
body: President Donald Trump said he does not know for sure whether Vice President JD Vance will run for president in 2028 , mere hours after Vance posted a lengthy social media post distancing himself from the Iran war.
Trump told reporters he spoke with Vance after Democrats flipped the House and Senate during the midterm elections on Tuesday.
“I speak to him about a lot of things, but I mean, we’ll see what happens. … You don’t know who’s talking about running,” Trump said while speaking from the White House ballroom construction site.
“You can have people running,” Trump continued. “You can have a lot of people. Maybe or a lot of people are running. Maybe nobody’s going to run. Maybe he won’t run. I don’t know who’s going to run.”

Vance’s social media post Wednesday was the first instance of him creating daylight with the administration’s policies, particularly the unpopular Iran war, in the wake of the midterm elections. High gas and diesel prices were top issues for voters across the nation. Polls showed Democrats would at least win the House on Tuesday. In the aftermath of the elections, Democrats won Senate seats in historically red states including Kansas and Texas. Democrats are poised to win at least 54 seats in the Senate and at least 234 House seats.

But with such a heavy loss, Vance may not have the primary field to himself in 2028. Sen. Ted Cruz (R-TX), who had already begun challenging Vance’s inevitability before the election, seems poised to run for president.
Early Wednesday morning, Vance posted on X that the “reason we lost is the war. The president himself said so last night.”
But Trump appeared to have no regrets about the war in his first appearance since the elections.

“I can tell you that as far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different,” Trump said. “We’ve totally broken their military. Their navy’s gone. Their air force is gone. Their anti-aircraft is gone.”
VANCE BLAMES IRAN WAR FOR GOP MIDTERM BLOWOUT
Although Trump did concede that he thought Vance’s comments were correct.

“I think it’s largely true because it drove the gasoline up a little bit, short term, and probably that’s probably it’s true,” he also said. “But at the same time, if I had it to do again, I’d have to do it again because long term, it’s the only answer. You can’t let Iran have a nuclear.”

articles.headline: 36 years later: Hungary opens Communist-era secret service files
keyFacts: Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government ordered the full release of Hungary's Communist-era secret police agent files.
The online publication will include names of informants and will be accessible to the public and historians.
Experts and officials noted the release could spark political consequences and renewed debate over historical guilt.
body: On November 4, 1956, tens of thousands of Soviet soldiers and tanks swept into Hungary, brutally suppressing the country's anti-Communist uprising. Decades of dictatorship followed, relying on Hungary's brutal secret police to keep the system in place.
Events on Nov. 4 this year represent something of a reckoning with this dark chapter of Hungarian history.

Prime Minister Peter Magyar's government is ordering the full release of the country's secret police "agent files," which contain the names of Hungarian state security informants, some of whom cooperated out of their own volition even as others passed on information unwittingly.

Magyar and his Tisza party had previously promised to make the "agent files" public if elected. Their release is an historic event, as it comes after over three decades of heated debate over how to handle such sensitive files. The decision to publish is also sure to spark further debate on Communist-era guilt and responsibility.
Release opposed for years

Hungarians have been calling for the release of the files for years. After the fall of the Berlin Wall in 1989 and the end of Soviet rule, civil rights activists and smaller Hungarian political parties said the files should be released. Demands for their publication were expressed repeatedly over following decades.

Yet Hungary's first post-Communist prime minister Jozsef Antall, a conservative, rejected the idea as did Viktor Orban's long-ruling Fidesz party. The latter blocked efforts to open the files, voting more than 30 times against such plans since 2010, according to Hungarian news platform Telex.

A partial release of state security files did occur in the 1990s, when the Hungarian parliament passed the so-called "agents law" in 1994. This required members of the government, members of parliament and certain public servants to undergo background checks to determine whether they had ever worked for the former state security services.
From 1997, Hungarian citizens have been able to view their own files and in 2003, permissions were expanded. But they have never been able to find out the names of informants.

The law relevant to the files contained provisions that were open to broad interpretation, which allowed government agencies such as the Ministry of Interior to prevent the transfer of files from the secret police to the Historical Archives of the Hungarian State Security, or ABTL, if they believed it would compromise national security.

Such a selective release of files not only prevented Hungarian society from learning the truth about its state security service, it also made it possible for files to be exploited in political power struggles, for example, by leaking compromising information about politicians to the public.
One such case involved former Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Medgyessy, who was exposed by the Fidesz-affiliated daily Magyar Nemzet in 2002 for having worked as a Communist-era secret agent.
Political fallout expected
Magyar's government is putting an end to this. From Nov. 4, databases containing all the names of, and key information about, informants will be made available online.

Additional databases will be released as well. They include one of the most extensive databases on individuals recruited to work for the Hungarian state security agency. Confidentiality provisions set out in the old "agent law" have also been scaled back, meaning significantly more files will likely be accessible in the future.

The upcoming release of data on up to 60,000 out of an estimated 150,000 secret police informants could have major political consequences. Even so, ABTL director Bendeguz Gergo Cseh recently cautioned that, "you can't believe everything the state security agencies and their files claim." Many documents were incomplete and not fully reliable and many files had been destroyed, he said.

Others are also skeptical about the release. Historian Janos M. Rainer, an expert on Hungary's dictatorship, told Telex that the publication would have made sense right after the fall of the regime. Releasing the files after all these years is more of a symbolic gesture, he argued.

Meanwhile historian Krisztian Ungvary, who has researched the state security files extensively, welcomes the upcoming publication. It will allow historians to pursue new research and society to engage in fresh debates, Ungvary told DW. He believes Hungary will benefit from such reflection, as "societal lies inevitably lead to a strained relationship with politics and the price we paid for that was 16 years of Fidesz rule."
Political reckoning
For Magyar, making this information public carries great significance. The idea of coming to terms with the past, especially the years of the Orban regime, is one of his favorite topics.

When the Hungarian parliament amended the law about the files in mid-September, Magyar wrote on Facebook that, "after a 36-year delay, the Hungarian parliament today decided, at the initiative of Tisza, to make the 'agent files' public. Fidesz did not support the motion. I wonder why?"
It was an allusion to the fact that many prominent figures in Fidesz' ranks and in Orban's inner circle were members of the Hungarian Communist party or secret police.
The most well-known of the latter is likely Jozsef Horvath, a former full-time employee of the department of Hungarian state security that was responsible for suppressing the domestic opposition.

Under Orban, Horvath worked as an intelligence officer and security advisor, and in 2024, he became the research director of Orban's Sovereignty Protection Office. This was an agency that exposed supposed enemies of the Orban regime, branding them " foreign agents ."
This article was originally published in German.

articles.headline: ‘Player I adore’ – Liverpool told academy star can reach top as rise with Rio Ngumoha and Trey Nyoni continues
keyFacts: Wales manager Craig Bellamy praised Liverpool academy forward Lewis Koumas, stating he has all the attributes to become a top player.
Koumas has played 13 times for Liverpool this season, making his Premier League and European debuts after previous loan spells.
Bellamy also described Scott Parker as a smart appointment following Parker's recent hiring as the new West Ham manager.
body: Wales manager Craig Bellamy could not speak higher of Liverpool’s academy star Lewis Koumas after his rise to the first team.
Koumas has become a regular for his nation as well as a breaking into the starting line-up for the Reds under Andoni Iraola .
The 21-year-old has played 13 times for Liverpool this season after breaking into the first team following two loan spells Getty
Alongside the highly-rated Rio Ngumoha and Trey Nyoni, who both started on Wednesday night in the Champions League , the 21-year-old has been rewarded with increased gametime this term.
So far this season under Iraola, Koumas has been handed his Premier League and European debut, playing 13 times already.
He has made seven top flight appearances for Liverpool , starting five times in all competitions, scoring and assisting one goal.
The forward spent the last two campaigns out on loan with Stoke City and Birmingham City , but he is now a key member of the Reds’ squad at Anfield.
And after another international call-up for the upcoming break, Wales boss Bellamy has piled praised on the youngster.
Bellamy tips Koumas for the top
Bellamy told talkSPORT in his press conference on Wednesday: “We saw it in the summer with us, when we brought him on.
“We always felt that Koumas has got all the attributes to be a really top player and obviously he hit the ground running in pre-season .
“The gametime is had is good game time and it’s only going to help us.
“From the period of when he played for us, going back to Liverpool and now leading into these games, he’s had good game time.”
The Wales manager added: “I have to be honest, the type of forward he is, the intensity he plays at I adore, it’s like if you could send me a forward, it’s him.
Koumas has become a regular for Liverpool under Iraola this season and his boss with Wales is also huge fan Getty
“He’s the type of player I adore. He dips in, dips out, looks to stretch, willing to get on the ball at any occasion.
“I honestly feel Liverpool are handling him incredibly well which is going to definitely benefit our country.
“So I’m really positive on the Koumas front at the moment.”
What else has Bellamy said?
Bellamy spoke very highly of Liverpool’s up-and-coming star Koumas, but he was also asked about another name in the news.
Scott Parker was appointed as the new West Ham manager on Wednesday and the ex-Hammer thinks it’s a perfect pick.
“I think it’s a really good appointment,” Bellamy said.
Parker has been appointed as the new West Ham manager after Nuno Espirito Santo was sacked earlier this week Getty
“I don’t like seeing a manager lose their role…you never feel comfortable with it, but we understand the reality of the world we live in.
“They’ve made a change and I look at Scott and it’s a real smart appointment, it make sense, and this is from the outside looking in.
“He’s a person whose been in that situation before, in similar circumstances with parachute payments, relegated from the Premier League and morale is a bit down.
“He was a brilliant player and an even better human being. He will grab everyone together, the players will adore him.
“The insight of playing for West Ham , it’s a special club. You don’t realise how big they are until you go to them.
“He’s been there and I see that as a huge advantage.”

body: Mauricio Pochettino has called in 25 players to take part in the pair of November international matches against Haiti in the CONCACAF Nations League quarterfinals.

A few of those 25 players are currently contracted to Major League Soccer clubs in the United States, but a larger majority of those individuals are playing in Europe after beginning their careers in MLS.

The surge in American talent overseas, many of whom originated in their home country as a young player before moving abroad, has pleased the USMNT head coach, who was especially congratulatory of MLS and its newfound ability to generate talent en masse and exporting it abroad.

Ahead of the two games against Haiti, where many young American players are sure to feature, Pochettino was effusive when it comes to the U.S. domestic league and how Americans are thought of across European clubs.
Mauricio Pochettino praises recent MLS development

"MLS to La Liga is a massive step," said Pochettino when asked about USMNT full-back Alex Freeman, who has risen to prominence under Pochettino as a previously unknown talent. Pochettino then used the example of Freeman's journey from MLS to Europe as a means to praise the American league's ability to develop talent and export it all over Europe.

"We need to congratulate ourselves, because to have this type of player arriving in the level they are performing and playing, that is what we want. You know the capacity of the MLS clubs and coaches, and all the different clubs how they are doing so well.

I think from outside of USA, I had the possibility to travel in Europe and be in USA, how the people are starting to see the quality of the players, and are starting to give value to the American player. But also they are also very interested in the way the clubs and federation work in USA. That is why talking about the quality of MLS coaches and MLS institute and also the federation, and the people who are working for a long time, we should congratulate everyone because I think they deserve the credit for all the talent that is appearing.

"Last week I was watching all the leagues in my house, and I see one goal from the Championship, from Premier League, from La Liga, from Bundesliga, from France. It's all American, American players, no? Performing in Italy, performing and scoring, that speaks very highly about the people that are working in MLS. articles.headline: Palantir CEO says it's pioneering an antiwar movement – while happily accepting defense dollars
keyFacts: Palantir CEO Alex Karp claimed the military software company is a pioneer of an antiwar movement because its products are built to deter conflict.
Palantir reported that its Q3 revenue rose 96 percent year-on-year to $2.31 billion while supporting military and intelligence customers.
Karp stated that Palantir has a moral imperative to dominate its industry and support war fighters while protecting civil liberties.
body: Alex Karp, CEO of US spy-tech company Palantir, used this week's historic US midterm election results to claim an unlikely mantle for a military software supplier: pioneer of an antiwar movement.

Palantir's Q3 revenue rose 96 percent year-on-year to $2.31 billion, although its shares fell 8 percent following the results, which it reported on Tuesday as US voters were delivering a resounding defeat for Republicans in the voting booth. For Karp, the figures represented "the reality that this moment has become a real focal point of understanding" and might help explain "what is happening in our society."
From the CEO's perspective, they not only reflected the company's financial performance, but also its overall "mission."

"That mission reason is we support your alpha [above average performance], we support your sovereignty. We support the war fighter. We are delighted that we can support the war fighter even more because we're making so much money. But we believe we have a moral imperative to be the dominant player in our industry," he told investors.
For Karp-watchers, this is familiar self-serving shtick: turn Palantir's work for military and intelligence customers into a moral crusade, and goad its critics along the way.

"There's this larger question of what does it mean to have a business that was built around what we believed and believe now is the most important mission in the world, supporting our war fighters, [and] bringing them home," he said.
None of this stops him presenting Palantir as a force for peace. "We see ourselves as the pioneers of a genuine and viable antiwar movement," he wrote in his shareholder letter .

He expanded on the point during the Q3 earnings call. "Our products are built to avoid war, meaning the adversary knows that they will have such pain inflicted upon them that, in fact, it's not worth going to war and also to create social cohesion because we're going to bring back our troops healthier, safer, undamaged and that makes our society much more effective," he said.

That antiwar pitch sits awkwardly alongside Karp's $1 million donation in December 2024 to MAGA Inc., the super PAC supporting Donald Trump. Trump subsequently launched a US military operation in Venezuela and went to war with Iran, repeatedly promising the latter conflict would be short-lived as it dragged on. Karp did not address either topic on the call.

Elsewhere, Karp claimed that Palantir "built products that would protect civil liberties and stop terrorism. If you don't stop terrorism, you're going to get a radical fringe on the right. If you stop terrorism without rights, none of us wants that."

That civil liberties pitch also invites scrutiny of Palantir's longstanding relationship with US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), whose treatment of people it targets and detains has drawn criticism from US judges .

Karp seems to enjoy the circus of controversy he and his colleagues have created. He also offered investors this insight: "The future is becoming the present and the present is now." Whatever that future holds, he seems confident Palantir has a moral imperative to invoice it. ®

articles.headline: SpaceX is snapping up hundreds of homes near its new flagship AI data center — but only if the owners agree to one incredible catch

body: - SpaceX reportedly offers to buy 418 homes near its AI facilities
- Homeowners face a lawsuit withdrawal condition attached to reported purchase offers
- Residents blame gas turbines for persistent noise and sleepless nights
SpaceX is reportedly seeking to purchase 418 homes in Colonial Hills, a Southaven neighbourhood close to its expanding artificial intelligence operations.
The properties stand close to a power station that supplies electricity to the company's computing facilities in the area.
The homes are near Colossus II, an artificial intelligence computing complex operated by MZX, a subsidiary of SpaceX.
Home purchases tied to an ongoing noise dispute
MZX has informed residents that it requires additional property for company operations, while Southaven Mayor Darren Musselwhite says some houses could accommodate incoming employees.
Real estate agents have reportedly contacted homeowners with purchase offers on behalf of the company, subject to conditions involving the litigation.
Reports say that homeowners must agree to withdraw from the pending lawsuit over gas turbine noise to qualify for the property buyout.

articles.headline: The midterms were a thumping rebuke of the US-Israel relationship

body: On the eve of a midterm election that ended in an unequivocal rejection of his brand of politics, even Donald Trump seemed to recognize that the US-Israel relationship has become a political liability.

Trump’s 11th-hour suggestion, on election morning, that he would cut military aid to Israel at the end of the year because, as he put it, “they don’t need it”, was condemned across the board – with pro-Palestinian advocates dismissing it as “desperate” and pro-Israel ones as “unserious”.

Trump’s suggestion that he would replace nearly $4bn in annual military aid with arms sales signaled little would change in practice – the funding would continue and it would be harder to track. But it was still a notable recognition by the president of just how much support for Israel has tanked against the backdrop of the latest war in Gaza, which has killed more than 70,000 Palestinian, been widely been described as a genocide, and reshaped US politics in ways unthinkable just three years ago.

Indeed, come January, the US House will include an army doctor who went on a medical mission in Gaza, a lawyer who was fired by her firm over a blogpost criticizing Israel’s war, a Jewish lawmaker who was recently detained by Israeli forces while helping Palestinians harvest olives in the occupied West Bank, and a community organizer who participated in a pro-Palestine student encampment and scored one of the primary season’s most stunning upsets under the banner “babies, not bombs”.

Pro-Palestinian candidates – including Palestinian-American ones – have won downballot races. And in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim to be elected to the US Senate, following a campaign that saw more than $40m spent by Aipac in an effort to defeat him, last-minute drama, and unprecedented levels of Islamophobic rhetoric and bigotry.

“The old bipartisan consensus on Israel is over,” Beth Miller, political director of Jewish Voice for Peace Action, said. Without that consensus in place, the next Congress could push a number of measures, from an arms embargo on Israel to sanctions against violent settlers and officials – though Trump would retain veto power to block them.

The vote was also a rejection of Trump’s war in Iran – something even JD Vance said on Wednesday was “obvious to almost everyone”. Foreign policy issues rarely determine US elections – that is, until those issues have a direct effect on Americans’ lives at home.

“Americans were reminded of the failures of the Iran war with every visit to the gas station and grocery store,” said Yousef Munayyer, head of the Palestine/Israel Program at the Arab Center Washington DC. “Israel is a central piece of that story.”

Across the country, and up and down the ballot, unabashedly pro-Palestinian candidates defeated pro-Israel ones despite groups like Aipa pouring tens of millions of dollars into a failed attempt to reverse Israel’s collapsing standing among US voters. Last month, Aipac acknowledged its open support was hurting pro-Israel candidates more than it helped them, and announced it would stop making direct endorsements and contributions – a remarkable admission even if one with little practical consequence.

The victories of El-Sayed and several other candidates whom the right sought to cast as antisemitic over their support for Palestinians also marked a significant rejection of the narrative that pro-Israel voices and the Trump administration have relentlessly advanced over the last three years – that criticism of Israel is, by default, antisemitic.

“They try to call you hateful if you believe that Palestinian kids should get to grow up in the land of their forefathers without being murdered by our tax dollars,” El-Sayed, who has continued to speak plainly about his support for Palestinians despite coming under enormous pressure over it, said during his acceptance speech. “If you believe in equal rights to peace, dignity, and self determination, that’s not hate, it’s love.”

In Michigan, El Sayed won a majority of Jewish voters, according to exit polls. Despite warnings that Jews would leave the Democratic party en masse over its shifts on Israel, J Street said its polling found that 72% of Jews voted for Democrats on Tuesday, even though the Republican party increased its share of the Jewish vote since 2024..
This does not mean that the Democratic party is unified on Israel and Palestine and or in opposition to foreign wars.

For decades, the party has “excluded or marginalized anyone whose progressive values extend to support for Palestine”, Lara Friedman, the president of the Foundation for Middle East Peace, said . “American voters, organizers, and a cohort of enormously talented candidates came together and kicked the door down.”

Matt Duss, executive vice-president of the Center for International Policy and a former foreign policy aide to Senator Bernie Sanders, said that the Democrats now must seize the opportunity to become the party opposed to war.

“Trump ran and won as an anti-war candidate in 2024, because unfortunately Democrats left that lane wide open for him,” he said. “The question is: Will Democrats finally get it? Will they finally realize that Americans are tired of war and want a new foreign policy?”

articles.headline: California voters overwhelmingly reject union-backed Prop. 44 crackdown on community health clinics
keyFacts: California voters overwhelmingly rejected Proposition 44, a union-backed ballot measure that would have required community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care.

Opponents, including the California Primary Care Association, raised about $39 million to defeat the measure, warning it could cause widespread clinic closures and force patients into emergency rooms.
Supporters from the SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West union argued the initiative would stop taxpayer-funded clinics from wasting money on excessive executive salaries.
body: California voters delivered a crushing blow to a controversial ballot measure that would have forced community health clinics to spend at least 90% of their revenue on patient care, rejecting the proposal amid dire warnings it could shutter hundreds of facilities.
Proposition 44 went down in flames Tuesday, with nearly 82% of voters opposing the measure as votes continued to be counted.

The landslide defeat marks another election setback for SEIU-United Healthcare Workers West, the powerful labor union behind the initiative, which argued that taxpayer-funded clinics were funneling too much money toward bloated executive salaries and other expenses instead of patients.
The proposal would have required nonprofit Federally Qualified Health Centers to devote at least 90% of their annual revenue to healthcare services or face hefty state penalties.

Clinics would have been limited to spending just 10% on administrative and other expenses, which would have been a dramatic shift from the roughly 80% they currently spend on services, according to the nonpartisan Legislative Analyst’s Office.
Supporters insisted the measure would crack down on wasteful spending and hold clinic executives accountable for how public money is used.
“Money should not be directed towards excessive executive compensation or other non-essentials that we have seen within … our clinic system,” union spokesperson Renée Saldaña told CalMatters.
But opponents painted a far more alarming picture, warning the sweeping restrictions could devastate California’s healthcare safety net, which serves an estimated 7 million low-income residents.
An analysis commissioned by opponents estimated clinics could face $1.7 billion in penalties during the first year alone, potentially triggering widespread closures and service cuts.

“By shutting down clinics, Prop. 44 will force millions of patients into already overcrowded emergency rooms — increasing wait times for everyone,” Dr. Susanne J. Spano, president of the American College of Emergency Physicians’ California chapter, warned in a California Voter Guide.

Critics also blasted the measure’s murky definition of healthcare spending, arguing that clinics could have been punished for investing in medical equipment, hiring support staff, expanding facilities or maintaining emergency reserves.
The initiative would have left California’s attorney general responsible for determining which expenses qualified as patient care.
State officials estimated enforcement would cost tens of millions of dollars annually, with affected clinics footing the bill through fees.
The bitter campaign also came with a hefty price tag.
Opponents, led by the California Primary Care Association, raised approximately $39 million to defeat the measure, more than double the $17 million collected by supporters.

“Today’s resounding defeat shows that health centers will not be bullied and that protecting the whole-patient, whole-community care we are known for will always be a priority,” association president Francisco Silva said in a statement to CalMatters.
The election also adds another defeat to the union’s ballot-box record after California voters rejected three previous union-backed initiatives targeting dialysis clinics in 2018, 2020 and 2022.
Meanwhile, the bruising fight has spilled into court.

The California Primary Care Association filed a lawsuit in September accusing the union and its president, Dave Regan, of using the ballot initiative to pressure clinics into accepting union bargaining demands.
The union has dismissed the allegations as “categorically false,” and the lawsuit remains pending.

articles.headline: Former Halo composer Marty O'Donnell loses election, then gets absolutely bodied by his opponent: 'The fight is finished'
keyFacts: Former Halo composer Marty O'Donnell lost his 2026 congressional election in a crushing defeat against Democratic incumbent Susie Lee.

body: It was a big night for Democrats in the US, as a "blue wave" saw the party retake control of Congress in what CNN called "a stunning blow to Trump." Among the night's big losers is former Halo composer Marty O'Donnell, whose run for Congress ended in a spectacular, crushing defeat—and then a dunk from his congressional opponent that can only be described as brutal.

O'Donnell began his political career in 2024, saying he "never wanted to be a politician" but felt compelled to do so by what he described as the deterioration of the US: "Big tech, big pharma, big media, big whatever—all trying to control big government in Washington DC."

That effort didn't work out so well—he placed fourth in the 2024 Republican primary for Nevada's third congressional district—but he tried again in 2026, this time with the support of US president Donald Trump, which O'Donnell enthusiastically welcomed despite previously calling Trump an "idiot." Well, winds and tides change.
Anyway, O'Donnell won the 2026 Republican primary, and then got in the ring with Susie Lee, the Democrat incumbent who's held the seat since 2019. It did not go well for him.
Hey, that happens sometimes—you think you got it, and then it turns out you don't actually got it at all.

But O'Donnell's Trump-toned campaign, complete with dire warnings about open borders, Marxism and the woke left, accusations of corruption leveled against Lee, embrace of the far-right commentariat, and occasional asides to remind everyone that he's absolutely not mad about being fired by Bungie, did not exactly endear him to his political opponents, or very many other people, really.
So after dismantling O'Donnell, the re-elected Lee—who seemed to largely ignore O'Donnell's rhetoric during the campaign—sent him off into the sunset with this:

I'm just a bystander on the scene—I'm not even American, much less a Democrat cheerleader. But holy cow. You can see that crater from orbit.
O'Donnell did not take Lee's farewell particularly well, which led to even more smoke in the comments.
I think this is one of those times were you have to just take it on the chin and move along. We'll see how that goes.

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

articles.headline: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's Navi actor reprises her role after 28 years, but it was a total accident due to Nintendo's blind auditions
keyFacts: Nintendo unintentionally cast the same actor twice, 28 years apart, to voice Navi in a new remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time.
Director HokWai Ng explained that blind auditions were held to ensure the new cast matched the original game's iconic vocal style.
Leaked credits and fan speculation indicate that Kaori Mizuhashi returned to voice Navi for the Japanese language version.
body: For The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time's shiny new remake, Nintendo unintentionally cast the same actor twice - 28 years apart - to deliver Navi's infamous "Heys!" and "Listens!"

The Switch 2's Ocarina of Time makes a pretty substantial change to the N64's Ocarina of Time, released almost three decades prior. There's proper voice acting this time, of course - not just grunts and murmurs and hyahs. But even when retroactively adding new things, Nintendo wanted to ensure the remake's cast matched the original's pretty faithfully, so the developer held blind auditions that eventually paved the way for one actor to reprise their role during Link's adventure.

"We felt that if we were going to improve the graphics so dramatically, the cutscenes needed to be fully voiced to match," director HokWai Ng explained in the most recent Ask The Developer blog. "But at the same time, we knew we shouldn't mess with established perceptions of how certain characters sound based on the original. Navi's "Listen!" is one example. Even someone who's never played The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time may have heard it before. We absolutely didn't want to change anything as iconic as that."
To maintain the original's nostalgic sounds and voices, Nintendo held blind auditions with the goal of finding actors who could recreate the "feel of the original game."

Series director Eiji Aonuma recalls that the team wanted to choose actors "based solely on which voices most closely resembled those of the original." And, who woulda guessed? "As fate would have it, one of the actors we selected had actually voiced the same character in the Nintendo 64 version. None of us saw that coming."

The duo didn't outright name which character they're talking about, but fans have long been speculating that Kaori Mizuhashi might be reprising her role as Link's trusty fairy companion Navi - at least, in the Japanese language version. A leaked online video of the game's credits now also confirms that Mizuhashi is back almost three decades later. I suppose it only makes sense that the person who most closely resembles Navi is Navi.
Chris Donlan called the new version an "astonishing remake" in his five-star Eurogamer Ocarina of Time review.

articles.headline: Brandon Sanderson’s Mistborn TTRPG Lays the Groundwork for His Next Series
keyFacts: Brotherwise Games published new tabletop role-playing books for Brandon Sanderson's Mistborn setting, spanning two eras and preparing for his upcoming novels.
Co-lead designer Meric Moir said the team collaborated closely with Sanderson and Dragonsteel Books to ensure game content remained canonical and avoided conflicting with future stories.
Brotherwise Games will announce its next Cosmere project at the Dragonsteel Nexus convention in December.
body: Last year, Brotherwise Games published a set of three tabletop role-playing game books set in the world of Brandon Sanderson’s epic fantasy series The Stormlight Archive. The company quickly followed up the project by announcing an expansion to the Cosmere RPG based on Sanderson’s Mistborn setting, and the new books reveal the true scope of the company’s ambitions.

The Mistborn Handbook, Mistborn World Guide, and Mistborn Legacy campaign are spread across two eras representing the two series Sanderson has written set on the planet Scadrial. It’s also laying the groundwork for Sanderson’s next trilogy in the setting.

“There was actually a moment about a third of the way into development where we might have had to just do Era One,” Meric Moir, co-lead designer of the Mistborn World Guide, told Polygon in a virtual interview. “Brandon Sanderson was really starting work on his Era Three novels, and as he got a clearer picture of what he was planning, he was very concerned about anybody adding to Era Two, and wanted to be very clear that we shouldn’t box him in.”

The Brotherwise team worked closely with Sanderson and Dragonsteel Books to expand some content for Era Two — which is set in a period akin to the Gilded Age — without interfering with the upcoming series, which will push the world’s timeline into the equivalent of the 1980s. They were able to add to the lore of how the godlike being Autonomy first became aware of Scadrial and established a secret organization called the Set.

“They started to give us a little bit more freedom to develop and pitch things that Brandon would review and say, ‘Yeah, actually, you know what? I didn't think of that. Let's go that way,’ or ‘I don't have a plan there. Why don't you come up with something, and then I can tell you if that'll work or not?'” Moir said.

Brotherwise co-owner and creative director Johnny O'Neal held weekly meetings with Dragonsteel to go over every piece of art in the books to ensure all the details were canonical and consistent. That’s especially important given the Mistborn World Guide is providing a first look at characters who will appear in AppleTV’s upcoming adaptation of Mistborn.

“I don't know what Dragonsteel is going to do, or what Apple is going to do, and I doubt they'll be constrained by us, but I can always hope that some of the things that Brandon has canonized with us will translate into a live-action thing, particularly the ethnicity of people in the Final Empire, like Dockson, who we got to canonize as Black, or Shan Elariel, who looks mixed race,” Moir said.

The Mistborn TTRPG books offer an enormous number of options for characters who can use 16 different metals for 32 powers, far more than the 10 types of surgebinding found in the Stormlight TTRPG books.

“Because they’re not developed for a game, some of them have far more depth than others, and some of them are just useless on purpose,” Moir said. “It became obvious early on that not every metal was going to have equal weight of mechanics.”
Gold allomancers can see possible versions of themselves, a power represented by just two talents. For comparison, using Iron to pull other metal objects is represented with a seven-talent tree.

“Brandon and his team have said ‘Sorry Brotherwise, the fans don’t know all the things that you could do with gold. There will be more, but we can’t reveal that,'” Moir said. “We can talk about what we know, and right now that’s small. One of the cool things about our system is we can just add on trees if we need to later as more information is revealed.”
The Mistborn TTRPG is bridging multiple worlds

The Mistborn rules also tease how worldhopping games could work if gaming groups want to explore the full breadth of the Cosmere. Burning Aluminum seems useless on Scadrial, but the art shows someone using it to negate the powers of a surgebinder from Roshar. Moir said the playtesting didn’t just focus on how the Mistborn abilities were balanced against each other, but how they would interface with the Stormlight books and other projects incorporating magic from Warbreaker and Elantris.

“Worldhopping is something that any Cosmere fan brings up in the first or second sentence when talking about the games,” Moir said. “Supporting that in a more robust way going forward is definitely on our radar.”
Moir is also the RPG director for Plotweaver, Brotherwise’s underlying rules system, and he’s been designing those rules with an eye towards what can be applied to the Cosmere.

“One very good example is vehicle rules,” Moir said. “We’re doing a science fiction setting so we’ve got spaceships, but the core of those rules will be modular. We can pull them back to Cosmere when Cosmere gets to its Space Age and we can customize it to be what Brandon Sanderson needs for telling an Isles of the Emberdark story.”
The Mistborn TTRPG is available today. Brotherwise will announce its next Cosmere project at the Dragonsteel Nexus in December.

articles.headline: An island in mourning: Tenerife processes death of De Miguel
keyFacts: Tenerife striker Jesus de Miguel died from injuries after a collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a match on Monday.
Hundreds of grieving fans, residents, and visitors have gathered at the stadium to leave flowers, candles, and tributes.
A further public tribute to honor De Miguel is planned for Saturday at 18:00 GMT, according to sports minister Poli Suarez.
body: - Published
As you arrive on the holiday island of Tenerife, there is a profound sense of grief, pain and disbelief at the death of footballer Jesus de Miguel.
The Canary island is in mourning for the Tenerife striker, who died from injuries sustained in a collision with FC Andorra goalkeeper Jesus Owono during a match on Monday.
The 30-year-old had quickly established himself as a club favourite, scoring 11 goals in his first season as Tenerife were promoted to the second tier of Spanish football.
But now the Heliodoro Rodriguez Lopez Stadium has become a shrine to the player, with hundreds of people gathering throughout the past few days to lay flowers, light candles and pay their respects.
Bouquets, rosettes sent by clubs from across Spain, prayer cards, photographs, children's drawings and scarves have been laid around the grounds outside gate nine.
It is a deeply moving scene. Fans and residents stand in silence, taking in the tributes.
Many are visibly tearful as the scale of the loss begins to sink in at the very place the incident happened.
'Football has no colours'
Among those paying their respects were Lisa and Lee, visiting Tenerife from Stoke-on-Trent.
They had arrived on holiday at the weekend and decided to attend Monday's match, hoping to experience Spanish football for the first time.
"We never expected something like this to happen," they told BBC Sport.
"We knew it was serious when the players surrounded him [De Miguel], but to see players crying and actually praying on the pitch was very emotional.
"When we found out the news the next day, it just really hit us."
The couple described the atmosphere inside the stadium as sombre and almost completely silent as spectators waited to understand what was happening.
"You always expect somebody to pull through," Lee said. "And then seeing the news the next day, it was just unbelievable."
They returned to the stadium on Wednesday to lay a Port Vale shirt among the tributes, wanting to show their support for the Tenerife community.
"Football has no colours," Lisa said. "If it was one of our players, we'd be heartbroken. They're part of your family."
'He's already a legend at the club'
For Carlos, a player with Tenerife's disability side Tenerife Foundation, the loss is particularly personal.
"Honestly, there are no words to describe him. He was incredible," Carlos said as he lay a flag on the ground.
He described De Miguel as a figure who had helped shape the club's recent history.
"He practically gave his heart and soul for the shirt. He's already a legend at the club because, after all, we were in a very difficult position a few years ago and he helped pull us out of it.
"Without him, I don't think we would be where we are today."
Carlos was at Monday's match and said he was left in shock by what unfolded.
"When I left the stadium I was trembling and I continued to feel that way for hours.
"Right now, we're incredibly hurt and very sad. I also want to send my support to his family, who I can only imagine must be absolutely devastated."
'The club is broken. Absolutely heartbroken'
The sense of loss has extended far beyond the stadium.
Poli Suarez, the Canary Islands' minister for education and sport, said Tenerife was in "complete mourning".
"Canarian sport has been left devastated," Suarez told BBC Sport. "The club is broken. Absolutely heartbroken."
Suarez also stressed that the thoughts of everyone were with De Miguel's wife, daughter and wider family.
"They are the ones suffering most directly from this loss, just as the Tenerife supporters are suffering," he said.
The government has pledged its support to the club, players and supporters, with Suarez describing De Miguel as a footballer who had become part of the Canary Islands' sporting history.
"The loss of Jesus de Miguel is now part of our history," Suarez said.
"Not only because of the circumstances of his death, but also because of the affection he always showed towards our island and towards his club."
A further tribute is planned for Saturday at 18:00 GMT, with supporters encouraged to come together to honour his memory.
"It will be an opportunity to show our affection and emotion, and to demonstrate our solidarity with the family," Suarez said.
"We want to show all our affection for Jesus de Miguel."
