articles.headline: Nintendo's main Switch cartridge supplier is leaving the ROM business
keyFacts: Nintendo's main Switch cartridge supplier, Macronix, is phasing out its ROM production business due to declining sales and a shift toward data center memory.
CEO Miin Wu confirmed the decision, noting that the ROM section now accounts for only five percent of the company's sales.
The change will not heavily impact Switch 2 cartridges because they use NAND flash memory, which Macronix is not phasing out.
body: Nintendo's main Switch cartridge supplier is leaving the ROM business
This is potentially terrible news for those who love physical media.

Nintendo's main Switch cartridges has plans to abandon the ROM portion of its business, according to reporting by the Taipei Times. The Taiwanese semiconductor and memory manufacturer Macronix is phasing out its ROM production, which was confirmed by CEO Miin Wu. This could spell bad news for gamers who love physical media.
Macronix just announced a record-high net profit of $337 million for Q3 2026, but Wu says many of its new customers have issued a "demand for NOR used in data centers." NOR is a type of flash memory.
1/4 Nintendo's main memory chip maker is quitting the Switch business

Macronix, which makes the ROM chips in Switch 1 and Switch 2 game memory cards, is phasing out that business. There will be no new ROM products, and Q3 is the last quarter it reports ROM sales separately.
— David Gibson (@gibbogame) November 4, 2026

The company's ROM business has actually declined by 39 percent over the past year. This section of Macronix now accounts for just five percent of sales, down from 26 percent this time last year. In other words, the financials just aren't there.

There is a silver lining here. Macronix may be Nintendo's main supplier of ROM for its cartridges, but it's far from the only entity helping to create physical Switch cartridges. Also, this doesn't impact Switch 2 cartridges in quite the same way. That's because the Switch 2 carts use NAND flash memory, a market segment that Macronix isn't phasing out.

However, this doesn't look too good for the long-term sustainability of physical game cartridges and discs. Digital products already account for 61.5 percent of Nintendo's software sales. This is even starker when you look at the other console manufacturers. Digital downloads make up around 85 percent of software sales on the PS5, which could account for Sony's recent move to end physical media sales altogether.

Both of the above numbers pale in comparison to Microsoft and its Xbox division. A whopping 96 percent of software sales are digital on Xbox platforms. The company has still yet to announce a plan to sunset physical media.

articles.headline: NYC's Mamdani says Abdul El-Sayed's Senate victory in Michigan 'means so much to so many'
keyFacts: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Wednesday that Abdul El-Sayed's Senate victory in Michigan means a great deal to many people.
El-Sayed defeated former Republican Representative Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim U.S. senator in history.
Mamdani stated that Democrats must use their newly regained power in the House and Senate to deliver tangible changes for working Americans.
body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said Wednesday that Abdul El-Sayed's Senate election victory in Michigan "is one that means so much to so many."
El-Sayed, who will become the first Muslim U.S. senator in history, toppled former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers in what was one of the most-watched contests of the election.

"I haven't spoken to him yet. I'm sure he is quite busy. I've had the privilege of speaking to him in the past, and I have to say that his election is one that means so much to so many," Mamdani said Wednesday.

"And to see to see that victory in the face that all that he had to reckon with over the course of that campaign, whether in terms of the extraordinary amount of money spent to oppose him or the racism and slander that he was met with on a daily basis, it is incredibly exciting to see as he said last night, that the good guys won," Mamdani added.
ABDUL EL-SAYED DELIVERS MAJOR BLOW TO GOP IN MICHIGAN AFTER BRUISING SENATE RACE
Mamdani added that "what last night showed us is that Americans are tired of being told that their needs are unrealistic by politicians who have been bought by the wealthiest people in the country.

"This country has elected a new generation of leadership, a generation with a mandate to lower the cost of living, to build, not bomb, to never betray the working people who entrusted them with power," he added. "And I hear often that the politics that we're fighting for here in New York City are not possible outside of city limits. And what last night showed us is that working people are the majority, whether we are speaking of Austin or Ann Arbor or Astoria, and it is time to put those same people first in our politics and last night shows us that it's possible to do so all across the country."
STATE OF PLAY: BLUE WAVE SWEEPS DEMOCRATS INTO POWER, WITH KEY RACES STILL HANGING IN BALANCE
Democrats regained control of the House and Senate during Tuesday's midterm elections, but Mamdani said that "it is not enough for us as Democrats to win power.

"We have to use that power to deliver change that Americans can feel in their wallets," he continued. "And to me, when you look at these campaigns, if we want to speak about James Talarico, he campaigned on a vision for universal childcare. If you want to talk about Keisha Lance Bottoms, well she campaigned on a vision of cutting red tape, to actually be able to build housing at the speed that's needed.

"If you want to talk about Jocelyn Benson, she campaigned on a moratorium for data centers. These, to me, are examples of the kind of specifics. But again, what I'm excited to see now is a recognition that the work is only just starting and that this has to be delivered for working people across the country," Mamdani declared.

articles.headline: A million people could gain health insurance in Texas after Democrats’ shocking win
keyFacts: Democrat Gina Hinojosa won the Texas gubernatorial race, and Democrats led enough elections to take control of the state House.
KFF estimates that 1.1 million low-income Texans would be eligible for health coverage if the state expands Medicaid.
Bee Moorhead of Texas Impact said Medicaid expansion bills will be filed November 9, though Republicans retain control of the Senate.
body: Gina Hinojosa speaks to supporters as she is announced as the next governor of Texas on election night, November 3, 2026. | ﻿Mikala Compton/The Austin American-Statesman via Getty Images

On election night in Texas, the impossible became possible. Democrats won the governor’s seat for the first time since the 1990s and appear to be on their way to securing control of the state House too . Those massive, unexpected wins have now opened the window for a major policy change that has long been closed: expanding Medicaid to more than a million low-income Texans.

The Affordable Care Act offers generous funding for states to expand Medicaid eligibility to 133 percent of the federal poverty level , which is about $21,000 for one person or $44,000 for a family of three. But the Supreme Court ruled in 2012 that states should have a choice about whether or not to accept the expansion. And even though many other GOP-led states decided to adopt it, Texas is one of the 10 that have steadfastly refused to extend Medicaid coverage to many of its poorest citizens — and it’s by far the biggest. KFF estimates that 1.1 million people in Texas would be eligible for Medicaid expansion, including 605,000 who have no other insurance options without it. In resisting expansion over the years, Republicans have argued that the Medicaid program was broken and already too expensive and that uninsured people should instead be able to get coverage by finding a job that offers health benefits.

New Democratic Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa pledged to pursue expansion if elected, framing it as a way to help the state’s children. If she can find a way to get the state legislature on board, Medicaid expansion in Texas would be one of the biggest direct consequences of 2026’s blue tsunami. Texas has the highest uninsured rate of any state in the country at 19 percent.

“We expect expansion to be a priority in the next legislative session. It’s a life-saver in the short term and a money-saver in the long term,” Lynn Cowles, director of health and food justice at the advocacy group Every Texan , told me in an email. “We’re excited to work with our new state cohort and committee chairs in January to make expansion a reality.”

There is still work to do. But Democrats are in the strongest negotiating position they’ve ever had in the Lone Star State. As of Wednesday morning, Dems were leading in enough races to take over the Texas House for the first time in more than 20 years. That will allow them to force a more serious conversation about expansion.

“You should expect to see Medicaid expansion bills filed on November 9, which is our first day for early bill filing,” said Bee Moorhead, executive director of Texas Impact . “Absolutely, it will be on the table.”

It’s not a guarantee because Republicans retain control of the state Senate. Still, there is some optimism that the sweeping Democratic victories in Texas and across the country could make the GOP more amenable to compromise.

Democrats will have one important ally in their fight: Texas hospitals, which have long supported expansion. Their political influence and the threat of Trump-approved Medicaid cuts leading to rural hospital closures — a major theme of Hinojosa’s campaign — could put pressure on Republicans to find a middle ground with the Democrats now in power.

But hospital leaders, having seen dreams of Medicaid expansion in Texas fall short before, aren’t declaring victory yet. Until some of the Texas Senate Republicans who have opposed Medicaid expansion in the past announce that they’re now open to a compromise, the GOP’s control of that chamber could be enough to continue blocking Medicaid expansion in Texas for the time being.

“Everything changed last night. But just because everything changed doesn’t mean everything changes,” John Henderson, president and CEO of the Texas Organization of Rural & Community Hospitals , told me. “We’re gonna have a different climate and different priorities in the next session. But some of these really ambitious policies still have obstacles to clear.”

Texans have been waiting for Medicaid expansion for a long time: A 2020 poll found that 69 percent of the state’s voters supported the policy. But Republican leaders, including now-ousted Republican Gov. Greg Abbott, refused to budge.

There is no guarantee that the stunning midterm results will finally break that logjam. It will require deft politicking by the new Democrats in power. But for the first time, there is real reason for hope.

articles.headline: Microsoft Teams Hack Report Shows Old-School Attacks Are Still a Thing
keyFacts: Microsoft reported that hackers used Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT personnel and trick users into granting remote access.
Microsoft stated it is introducing AI-powered phishing detection and other features while advising users to verify external identities.
Expert Yu Cai said that human-led social engineering attacks remain a major cybersecurity threat despite the focus on AI.
body: Over the last year, the public has been trained to view the biggest new wave of emerging cyberthreats as AI-driven. In fact, frontier AI models accelerating the pace of cyberattacks — and even jumping ahead so far that the models have to be paused in the case of Anthropic’s Mythos — have driven the cybersecurity conversation recently.

But a recent report from Microsoft detailing how hackers used its Teams software to infiltrate corporate systems shows that human hackers are still using social engineering scams to fool other humans into doing their dirty work.

According to the report, “threat actors used Microsoft Teams messages and calls to impersonate IT or help desk personnel and socially engineer users into granting interactive remote access, primarily through Quick Assist.” Once they were granted access by unsuspecting workers, the hackers were able to set up software using Python, Bun or Java runtimes, open up networks and grant themselves authentication, giving them free rein over corporate systems.
More from CNET

In order to open the door to all that activity, however, a human had to grant access to the intruder. “Both incidents began with Teams phishing messages and calls that impersonated support personnel,” the report stated. “The social engineering persuaded a user to establish an attacker-controlled remote session, primarily by guiding the user to open Quick Assist and provide the connection code. This gave the attacker hands-on-keyboard access to the workstation.” Presumably, the employees who granted access thought the people on the help desks reaching out were just doing their jobs to keep their workplaces safe and operations running smoothly.
Microsoft suggests verifying external IDs

In an email to CNET, a representative for Microsoft said the company is introducing AI-powered phishing detection that it says “uses conversation context to identify phishing and social engineering in higher-risk messaging scenarios, particularly first-contact chats with external users.”

The change was listed as part of Microsoft’s roadmap for the software, which was revealed last month. Teams will also add ways to report suspicious guest invitations and blur QR codes sent by external senders, according to that roadmap.

However, a lot of the burden of making sure these hackers don’t get through falls to companies and their employees. “Users should exercise caution with external connection requests and messages, including verifying a sender’s identity and requests before acting on them,” Microsoft’s spokesperson said. “Administrators can also block external Teams users and specify which users in their organization are permitted to chat or meet with people outside the enterprise.”
Human-led attacks can harness AI, too

Yu Cai, associate director of the Institute of Computing and Cybersystems at Michigan Tech, said social engineering attacks are definitely still widespread. “AI may be changing the cybersecurity landscape, but it hasn’t replaced the human hacker. Human-led social engineering attacks remain a major cybersecurity threat, even as AI cyber attacks continue to get the bulk of today’s headlines,” he said.

But Cai said AI attacks and human-led attacks aren’t necessarily in separate buckets. AI can help make social engineering hacks more convincing by providing tools like voice cloning or deepfake videos.

In the case of the Microsoft Teams hacks, Cai said that what was most surprising was how simple the approach was to gain access. “This is a great reminder that sophisticated attacks don’t necessarily have to begin as sophisticated hacks,” he said. “This Microsoft incident wasn’t caused by any vulnerabilities in the Teams software, but by employees naturally placing trust in communications that come through the tools they use each and every day.”

articles.headline: Researchers asked people to use AI chatbots for election info – results were mixed
keyFacts: Researchers asked nearly 2,500 people in 35 states to query AI chatbots about the midterm elections to study political usage.
Most participants asked for basic facts, but 36% asked chatbots to help them choose a candidate based on personal priorities.
Researchers said the next step is determining how accurate and unbiased model responses are and whether recommendations match user needs.
body: ZDNET’s key takeaways
- Americans use AI to search for information – including elections.
- Voters ask chatbots for basic election information and candidate recommendations.
- AI systems can hallucinate and add layers of bias to political information.
Most search tools now put a layer of AI between you and the information you’re looking for, especially Google.
What voters asked chatbots

The researchers asked nearly 2,500 people in 35 states with Senate races to query ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, or Gemini about the election. Participants in the study, which ran for a few weeks in October leading up to the Nov. 3 midterm elections, were adults who already use chatbots weekly.

Most users asked chatbots for basic facts about the election, including who was on the ballot. But 36% asked a chatbot to help them pick a candidate to vote for, often by describing their priorities and asking the chatbot to assess which candidates aligned with them.

The former query has slightly less room for error, because the internet has a ton of data on the basic facts of an election, such as who is running where. Chatbots interpreting candidate positions, on the other hand, is a bit more dicey, and relies significantly on the sources a chatbot uses (a statement from a candidate’s own website, for example, is more reliable than a social media clip of an opponent characterizing them in a certain way).
In one example, a user asked ChatGPT to give them the “pros and cons” of each candidate in Virginia, an inherently subjective question.
When it came to recommending candidates, chatbots varied widely.

“When users asked who to vote for but had not yet said anything about themselves, only Grok regularly recommended a candidate, in 14% of chats,” the researchers wrote. “Once users shared their views, ChatGPT recommended a candidate in 79% of chats and Claude in 40%, with Grok and Gemini in between.”
AI and elections

Pew Research found that 42% of US adults surveyed use chatbots to search for information. That’s a broad umbrella that can include election information — but Pew also found that only 8% of US adults reported using chatbots to find election-related information in this year’s election.

What those users are looking for matters, though. Pew found that of that group, 76% were inquiring about where candidates stand on certain issues, and 71% were fact-checking information they’d heard about candidates or issues.
Also: OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs

Given that chatbots are still not reliable summarizers, the nature of these questions poses a misinformation risk if users don’t also check a chatbot’s linked sources. An overwhelming majority of users don’t, at least when it comes to Google’s AI Overviews. At least one study found AI platforms gave users “outdated or inaccurate” information that could mislead voters in some cases by missing a deadline or failing to mention a step about voting logistics.

This election cycle was particularly plagued by AI-generated deepfakes and misinformation as tools have become much more sophisticated since the 2024 election. OpenAI and Anthropic reportedly set up election “war rooms” to monitor misuse and information accuracy, according to exclusive reporting by Politico and Semafor.

While an August study from the Brennan Center for Justice found that chatbots did push back surprisingly well against certain falsehoods related to election disinformation campaigns, it also found that AI models easily generated “misleading election-related images and video” when asked.
“Many of their safeguards for preventing this were ineffective, inconsistently applied, or functionally absent,” noted the study, which tested ChatGPT, Gemini, Grok, Meta AI, Runway, and Flux.2.

Apart from these factors, however, there is a broader theme in AI use that is equally consequential for civic engagement: cognitive offloading. The political media landscape can already be dense and hard to parse for a voter trying to stay informed. Layering a chatbot — which has opaque training data sets, filters, and other settings determined at the discretion of AI labs — on top of that information search process can further muddy the waters while appearing like a convenient and neutral summarizing tool.
Why this study matters

While some studies test how AI chatbots respond to election questions by using standardized questions, this approach let users themselves engage with chatbots as they normally would. While the Yale researchers’ queries and standardized study queries show a lot of similarities, the distinction is valuable for evaluations.
“This is a small step toward evaluations that measure AI’s political influence on the questions users actually ask,” the researchers noted.

Outside of users self-reporting what they asked a chatbot, only AI labs have records of what users are really asking about elections. In October, Anthropic analyzed 250,000 conversations with Claude and determined people “rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for,” finding that “0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting,” though it expected election-related queries to increase closer to Nov. 3.
Also: 6 AI agent workflows I use to hand off everyday tasks

“More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations,” Anthropic’s report said.

The Yale researchers said the next step for a study like theirs is determining how accurate and unbiased models are in their responses, as well as what models learn about users, and whether their recommendations actually match users’ needs.

“In multi-turn chats, users often answered the chatbot’s questions, and those answers led to its recommendations. The questions a model asks shape what users tell it and what it recommends,” the researchers explained.

articles.headline: "Arkane is profitable," say Marvel's Blade developers in fiery new statement, "just not profitable enough for Microsoft"
keyFacts: Unionised workers at Arkane Lyon stated that Microsoft caused the studio's economic difficulties by imposing a hiring freeze and withholding resources.
The workers asserted that Arkane is profitable but does not meet Microsoft's profit expectations, leading to potential studio closure and low redundancy offers.
Negotiations between Microsoft and Arkane workers regarding the studio's future and redundancy terms are ongoing until December 13th.
body: Unionised workers at Dishonored developers Arkane Lyon have published a fresh statement about the progress of negotiations with Microsoft over the studio's potential closure. Aside from calling on Xbox management to make a redundancy offer proportionate to Microsoft's colossal market value, they accuse the parent company of creating the very economic conditions cited as a reason for closing Arkane, and thereby "sabotaging" development of the forthcoming Marvel's Blade.

Shared by French union Le Syndicat des Travailleureuses du Jeu Vidéo, the (slightly shonky) official English translation of the statement begins by insisting that "work on Blade is going fine" and that the game will measure up to previous Arkane Lyon releases, despite the stress of trying to pin down a new owner for the company, after Microsoft announced plans to part ways with Arkane and several other studios back in July. It then takes Microsoft to task for making an "outrageously low" redundancy offer to Arkane's workers, and further accuses the Xbox company of essentially setting Arkane up to fail by imposing a hiring freeze and depriving the studio of resources.

"Microsoft chose to justify the closure on economic reasons," the workers write. "But Microsoft is actually why those economic reasons even exist." It asserts that Microsoft froze hiring "for 19 months, which artificially caused delay and additional cost", only to then use those delays and extra costs "as a reason to close down the studio". It also claims that Microsoft have "systematically" deprived Arkane of cash, by means of corporate mechanisms the statement doesn't make wholly clear. "Even this closure itself is done against any financial logic, as closing Arkane today would probably be more expensive than finishing the game," the statement adds, without going into detail.

"The truth is that Microsoft based its decision only on stone cold and inhuman logic, in which our lives, projects and dreams are voided, so we can better serve Microsoft’s short term financial goals," the workers continue. They accuse Microsoft of "the brutal application of a never-ending search for maximum profit optimization", citing years of mass layoffs across the Xbox company together with the recent voluntary buyout offering. "Arkane is profitable," they add. "Just not profitable enough for Microsoft."

The workers want a "solid offer" from Microsoft regarding the studio's post-Xbox future, declaring that "when the company who decided that Arkane has to shut down is, according to many sources the most profitable in the world, with a net profit of more than 133 Billions of dollars in the past years, it would be the bare minimum to ensure that the redundancy plan offered by Microsoft is on [par] with their means."

They list a few specific demands. Firstly, they want Microsoft to go beyond the work council consultation mandated by French law, "and actually give employees representative & unions a say in the discussion to choose a potential buyer". They want Microsoft to create a fund to protect workers, if they're fired by any hypothetical acquiring company "for economic reasons" in the 24 months after the deal.

If Arkane have to close, the unionised workers call on Microsoft "to release funds commensurate with Microsoft’s status as a corporation, to make sure that the workers are compensated in line with the loss suffered". They'd like a redundancy payment of €200,000, two years of "redeployment support", a package of "shared resources for training and studio creation", including a residual bonus, and "compensation up to the redundancy payment for independent workers’ contract breach", to safeguard the livelihoods of freelancers and contractors.

The warring parties at Xbox and Arkane have until 13th December this year to figure out a deal. Reportedly, Ubisoft are among those looking to buy Arkane - a source of some concern, given that Ubisoft have also recently closed a number of studios and laid many people off. I'm not sure I'd be waving my wallet around if I were using my other hand to sign pink slips.

- Microsoft reportedly add Arkane and their Blade game to the potential shuttering pile

articles.headline: People say they want small smartphones—the Enough Phone will put that to the test
keyFacts: Enough Phone is beginning preorders for its new device, which features a compact 5.3-inch screen designed to test consumer demand for smaller smartphones.
The device includes mid-range specifications, a user-replaceable battery, and a choice between standard Android 17 and the de-Googled OdysseyOS.
Carrier support, waterproofing ratings, and final battery capacity remain unclear, though the company aims for broad global 5G support.
body: The first modern smartphones had 3.5-inch screens, which can be hard to remember in today’s world of gargantuan glass slabs. Sure, people talk about wanting smaller phones, but will they buy one? Enough Phone is betting they will. The company will begin taking preorders for its first device today, which is built around a petite 5.3-inch screen that is apparently the smallest it could find with decent performance metrics.

The company’s cheeky name is reflected in its approach to phone design. A flagship killer this is not, but it’s probably “enough” for most people. It has a mid-range MediaTek processor, a single rear-facing camera, a polycarbonate body, and a fingerprint sensor in the power button.

With that compact screen, the Enough Phone will be dwarfed by almost every existing smartphone. While it’s a bit thicker, the device has almost the same footprint as the iPhone 13 Mini. Thinness takes a hit, as the designers have opted to make the battery user-replaceable. Like the Fairphone, you’ll just have to remove a few screws to get the back cover off.

On the software front, the device will offer a choice. You can get an Enough Phone with a standard Google-certified build of Android 17, which is probably what most people will choose. It also supports OdysseyOS, a streamlined, de-Googled version of Android that behaves like a dumbphone (it doesn’t even have a browser).

Some minor details are still up in the air. The designers aren’t yet sure about waterproofing and durability ratings, and the battery capacity could change. But they hope that spec will go up, not down, if it changes at all. Carrier support is also unclear right now. It will be an unlocked 5G phone, and the company is aiming for “broad global support.” But if you’re on a restrictive carrier like Verizon, you may be out of luck.

articles.headline: Final Fantasy’s Yoshinori Kitase Teases What’s Next for Square Enix, Says Company Will Prioritize New Games Over Remakes
keyFacts: Square Enix producer Yoshinori Kitase stated that the company will likely prioritize investing in new titles moving forward over remakes.
Kitase said he is open to the possibility of future games or TV series inspired by Final Fantasy stories.
Kitase noted that while fans often request a Final Fantasy VI remake, he does not plan to work on another remake anytime soon.
body: Final Fantasy VII Revelation is still months away, but a prominent voice in the Final Fantasy universe is already teasing what’s next for publisher Square Enix after the game releases next year.

I spoke exclusively with Yoshinori Kitase, who serves as producer of the Final Fantasy VII Remake trilogy, director of the original Final Fantasy VII (along with Final Fantasy VI, VIII, X, and Chrono Trigger), and brand manager of the Final Fantasy franchise at Square Enix, at the Lucca Comics & Games Festival 2026.

We spoke at length about Kitase’s decades-long involvement in the Final Fantasy franchise, and why he’s ready to turn the page. During the conversation, Kitase shared plans about what’s next for Square Enix, if he’s still interested in film adaptations, and which Final Fantasy game fans inside and outside the company want to remake next.
Square Enix Will Likely Invest in New Titles Moving Forward

IGN: I want to of course talk about Final Fantasy, but also Square Enix in general. Square Enix is very famous for both new IP and also remakes. How do you balance that as a company? Are they both equally important to the company at this moment and also moving forward?

Yoshinori Kitase: I think that mainly we are more likely to invest in new titles and new games, but at the same time, for example, this time with the [Final Fantasy VII] remake, there was me and other creators who worked on the original game, which we had really strong feelings towards. And we really wanted to create something new related to the old game to allow new users to play and to know the appeal of this game as much as the old users who play the old game. So there might be different cases like this one where the company is willing to invest in remaking old projects and other kinds of games like it happened this time.
The One Quality That Makes Final Fantasy Special
IGN: Speaking of Final Fantasy, you've worked on a lot of Final Fantasy games. Is there one quality that you think that makes Final Fantasy special or popular?

Yoshinori Kitase: I think that the main thing would be the characters who are part of the game and the way they are developed throughout the game. So if I have to take just one thing that makes the game special, I would say [it is] the characters of the game and the way they are developed.

Also, one more thing I think would be the fact that, originally, the aesthetic of the game was really influenced by European culture. And then as the time went by, the game took more and more things from the Japanese culture, because the other creators working on the game and I, we grew up in Japan of course, so we were in contact with comics and anime and Japanese comics. And that started having a main role in the development of the game.

So I think thanks to the original influence from European culture and then the influences from Japanese culture, it helped create something which is unique in its genre. And I think that might be something that's really appreciated by the fans all over the world.
Square Enix Wants to Return to the World of Film

IGN: Final Fantasy and other Square Enix titles have been adapted in various formats: movies for example. Is that something that is still important to the company and is that something that the company will be looking to do in the future?

Yoshinori Kitase: Given the fact that we created this game, the remake of Final Fantasy VII, which explored the world of Final Fantasy VII way more than the original version, I think that it would be nice to have in the future games or TV series inspired by the story of Final Fantasy. And I don't see why that should not be a possibility in the future.
Kitase’s Reaction to Clair Obscure: Expedition 33

IGN: Speaking of things that have been inspired by Final Fantasy, a recent very popular game was Clair Obscure: Expedition 33. I'm wondering if you have any opinions about turn-based combat in RPGs. Has Square Enix thought about that? What is your opinion on big games like that are inspired by your work?

Yoshinori Kitase: To be honest, I know the game. I spoke with the creators and I'm actually very happy about the fact that they have been so inspired by Final Fantasy and they created a new game from that. And also, I was inspired by movies and in particular by Star Wars when I was young.

So I took inspiration from many things I was interested in when I was younger and I used that inspiration to create my games. So I think it's beautiful that there's this kind of cycle where we inspire each other and we take things from each other's games. I think it's something beautiful and it should be like that.
Two Star Wars Inspirations for Final Fantasy Confirmed

IGN: Since you were such a fan of Star Wars, is there a particular scene or character or theme from that universe that directly inspired something, whether it be in Final Fantasy or any of your other works?

Yoshinori Kitase: I think I like Star Wars so much that I was afraid of using anything related to [it] because I was worried that it became something just exactly identical to Star Wars. So I don't think there's something from the movie that I used directly as an inspiration for my games.
IGN: So it was more just being a general fan and absorbing those stories?

Yoshinori Kitase: Actually, something that I used as an inspiration inside the game was the name of a character in Final Fantasy VI. I wasn't sure about the name I was going to use for those characters. And I ended up using the names of characters from Star Wars, [Biggs and Wedge].

I ended up using [those names] as an homage to Star Wars. One more that came to my mind is from Final Fantasy X, where I had to create [Blitzball] for the game inside the fantasy setting. And I used an idea from Star Wars Episode 1 where there's this [pod] race and the fact of using sport inside a fantasy context, I took this idea directly from Star Wars.
Kitase’s Favorite Final Fantasy Game

IGN: This may be an impossible question. But of all the Final Fantasy projects that you’ve worked on, do you have one that is your favorite? Do you have one that you look back on and are most satisfied with?

Yoshinori Kitase: This is a very difficult question, but I think actually it might be Final Fantasy VII just because the same thing: each episode changes every time. But in this case, I have been handling these games ever since the original came out in 1997. Up until today, it's been 30 years and I've been working on the same characters, on the same storyline. So I think this might be the one I feel more attached to.
Does Kitase Want to Remake Another Final Fantasy Game?

IGN: Obviously, the Final Fantasy VII remake has been a huge project spanning many, many years. If you had a blank check; if you had no challenges or restrictions to reimagine another classic Square Enix game in the way that you have done with Final Fantasy VII, do you have one in mind?
Yoshinori Kitase: It's a very difficult question because if I say, "I will remake this game, in five seconds all the world is going to wait for the remake of this game." So it's very difficult.

I was very fulfilled by the development of the Final Fantasy VII remake. And at the moment I would like to create new games, but I don’t have any particular feeling towards any kind of remake for a while. So I don’t think I will work on another remake anytime soon. But inside the company and also among the Final Fantasy fans, there's been many people asking for a remake of Final Fantasy VI, so who knows?
What Type of Game Kitase Wants to Make Next
IGN: Are there any types of stories that you haven’t gotten to work on yet that you’re interested in exploring in your next chapter?

Yoshinori Kitase: The new generations are very fond of battle games, not much centered on the story, but on the battle action. Maybe in the future I would like to try and explore that kind [of game] without losing the characteristics of a Final Fantasy story. Maybe trying to create something more focused on that. That might be a new challenge since the new generation seems to be very interested in this kind of game.

articles.headline: Abdul El-Sayed welcomes Trump's plan to cut Israel aid, calls for end to arms sales
keyFacts: Democrat Abdul El-Sayed defeated Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate.
El-Sayed welcomed President Trump's plan to end roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel.
El-Sayed called for a complete halt to U.S. weapons sales to Israel and questioned military support for other countries.
body: Abdul El-Sayed welcomes Trump's plan to cut Israel aid, calls for end to arms sales
Democrat Abdul El-Sayed made history in Michigan, defeating Republican Mike Rogers to become the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate as his party reclaimed control of Congress.

The 42-year-old former public health official campaigned on lowering costs, Medicare for All and getting corporate money out of politics. Rogers, backed by President Trump, repeatedly attacked El-Sayed over his Muslim faith and opposition to U.S. military aid to Israel.

But Israel and the war in Gaza became a defining fault line in the race. Haley Stevens, whom El-Sayed defeated in the Democratic primary, endorsed Rogers just days before the election amid a bitter dispute over Israel.
After a campaign marked by heated disagreements over Israel, El-Sayed now finds himself on the same side of an issue as Trump.
The president announced plans to end roughly $4 billion in annual military aid to Israel by the end of the year, though he offered no details on how the cuts would work.
Speaking to Morning Edition after his victory, El-Sayed welcomed the proposal.
"I think the president is actually right on this policy," he said. "I'd also like to see us stop selling weaponry that gets used to do the worst things, including genocide and apartheid, to Israel."
The U.S. provides Israel with $3.8 billion in annual military aid under an agreement that runs through 2028.
His argument goes beyond Israel. El-Sayed also questioned U.S. military support for Egypt, Saudi Arabia, Jordan and Pakistan, saying American tax dollars should be spent at home.
Winning Michigan's Senate seat, however, doesn't mean every division within his party has disappeared.

During a visit to Michigan before the election, NPR's Michel Martin heard concerns about El-Sayed from some Jewish and Black voters. Asked whether he still had work to do to win their support, El-Sayed said the election results challenged that narrative.
"There's always more work to do. There's always more to build. There's always more conversations to have," he said.

The digital version was edited by Treye Green.

articles.headline: U.S. Marine dies in Japan during training, military says
keyFacts: A United States Marine died in a training incident at Camp Schwab in Okinawa, Japan, the military announced Wednesday.
The unnamed Marine belonged to the 3rd Marine Division and died on Tuesday, according to the military.
The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation, the 3rd Marine Division stated.
body: A United States Marine has died in Japan, following a “training incident,” the military said in a statement Wednesday.

The unnamed Marine was undertaking training at Camp Schwab in Okinawa, Japan’s southernmost prefecture, the statement said. The area is home to a large U.S. military presence and bases that serve as a regional hub in the Indo-Pacific.

The Marine who was with the 3rd Marine Division died Tuesday and will not be named until 24 hours after the individual’s family has been notified, the 3rd Marine Division said in a statement Wednesday.
“It is with heavy hearts that 3rd Marine Division announces the death of a Marine following a training incident at Camp Schwab, Okinawa, Japan, on Nov. 3, 2026,” the statement said.
“The circumstances surrounding the incident remain under investigation,” it added. “We express our deepest condolences to the family and loved ones of our Marine.”

Okinawa was under U.S. occupation following World War II until it was handed back to Japan in 1972. Today, the U.S. population on the island is nearly 80,000, with nearly 30,000 being active duty troops from all four branches of the armed forces, though the Marines make up the bulk of the forces.

Separately, Secretary of State Marco Rubio last month pledged to cooperate with Japanese authorities investigating allegations that a U.S. Marine murdered a woman in Okinawa. The case sparked widespread protests and led to a U.S. military curfew and mandatory training in standards and discipline.
Lt. Gen. Benjamin Watson, commander of the III Marine Expeditionary Force, said at the time that serving on the Japanese island “comes with responsibility.”

articles.headline: Iran says U.S. election results show Americans reject the war
keyFacts: Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday that U.S. midterm election results showed Americans reject the war launched against his country.
President Trump stated Tuesday night that he has no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran despite ongoing attacks in the Strait of Hormuz.
Four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while transiting the Strait of Hormuz, according to Iran's Revolutionary Guard on Wednesday.
body: What to know about the Iran war today:

- Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday that the U.S. midterm election results reflected Americans' rejection of President Trump launched against his country. Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf added a warning that if Mr. Trump does not heed the message from American voters, it will bring "a Nightmare."

- President Trump acknowledged Tuesday night that the war with Iran was partially to blame for the GOP's resounding midterm elections losses. But Mr. Trump told The Wall Street Journal he didn't regret the conflict and added he "would have done it again."

- Despite signs of a to reach a peace deal, ships continue to come under attack in the Strait of Hormuz. Four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while transiting the waterway, Iran's Revolutionary Guard said Wednesday.
Trump says U.S. has no immediate plan to strike Iran, despite being "locked and loaded"

President Trump told the Financial Times newspaper on Tuesday evening that he had no immediate plans to order new strikes on Iran, after keeping the option on the table for weeks ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.

"We seem to be getting everything we want," the FT quoted Mr. Trump as saying, referring to the current stalemate with Iran. While major fighting stopped weeks ago, the standoff has seen the Islamic Republic continue threatening and attacking commercial ships in the Strait of Hormuz, which in turn has kept global oil prices 60% to 70% higher than they were before the war started, driving up consumer costs across the globe.
Asked whether there would be a new attack on Iran later this week, Mr. Trump said "we're locked and loaded if we need to go, but there may be no reason for it."

Despite the impasse, the president claimed the current circumstances were "brilliant," with oil still reaching global markets from the Persian Gulf, including under U.S. military escort through the Strait of Hormuz.
"If you think about it, we haven't really had a war with them in a long time. Six months, maybe more," asserted Mr. Trump.
China says avoiding more conflict in Middle East a "top priority"
China's foreign ministry said Wednesday that avoiding a resumption of the conflict between Iran and the U.S. was a "top priority" in its diplomatic efforts in the region.

"The top priority is to avoid the resumption of hostilities in the Middle East that would bring disaster to the region's people," Chinese Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning told reporters in Beijing.

China will "support Iran and the U.S. in resolving disputes through negotiations, promote finding a political settlement to the Yemen issue, to help reach a proper and comprehensive solution for the opening of the Strait of Hormuz," she added.
China is an economic ally of Iran. Chinese purchases of Iranian crude oil amount to nearly 45% of the Iranian government's budget, according to a U.S. government report from March 2025.
Later this month, Beijing will send its Middle East envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia for visits "aimed at promoting peace talks (and) easing tensions," the foreign ministry said Wednesday.
CBS/AFP
Lebanese prime minister warns of "risks of renewed war," and of Lebanon being dragged in again

In a message seemingly directed at the Iran-backed group Hezbollah, Lebanon's prime minister warned Wednesday against any moves that could pull the country into renewed fighting between Iran and the U.S. and Israel.

"Faced with the risks of renewed war in the region, I renew my warning of the dangers of dragging Lebanon into a new senseless adventure in service of outside interests," Nawaf Salam said on Wednesday, without explicitly mentioning Hezbollah.

Southern Lebanon has been a major front in the interlinked regional conflicts, with fighting between Iran's Hezbollah allies and Israel's military driving tens of thousands of people from their homes and killing almost 9,000 since Oct. 7, 2023, according to the Lebanese health ministry.

Hezbollah, long a powerful political and paramilitary force in the country, pulled Lebanon directly into the war with Israel by launching strikes on the Jewish state in support of Hamas after the 2023 terror attacks sparked the war in Gaza, and then by firing rockets and missiles in support of Iran after joint U.S.-Israeli strikes commenced on Feb. 28.

The Lebanon conflict has proven to be a major sticking point in negotiations between the U.S. and Iran, as Tehran has consistently rejected any peace deal with Washington that does not also end fighting in Lebanon and Gaza.

A fragile ceasefire agreement reached between Israel and Hezbollah in June has halted most large-scale fighting between the two sides, but Israeli forces still occupy a large section of southern Lebanon, and there are sporadic attacks by both sides.
"We do not accept the country again becoming a theater for the conflict of others," Salam added, saying Lebanon had "already paid a heavy price."

President Trump threatened repeatedly ahead of the U.S. midterm elections to renew strikes on Iran, but he told the Financial Times as the results came in Tuesday evening that he had no immediate plans to order attacks.
CBS/AFP
Four tankers catch fire while transiting Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military says
Four oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while attempting to pass through the Strait of Hormuz, Iran's military said Wednesday, after it warned no one would benefit from a return to war.

"Four non-compliant oil tankers attempting to pass through the prohibited passage south of the Strait of Hormuz were destroyed after striking naval mines and are still burning," Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps said in a statement quoted by state TV.
"Two other non-compliant ships or vessels have also been halted," they said
The attacks come even as a diplomatic push is underway aimed at reaching a deal between the U.S. and Iran. Indirect talks via Qatari, Pakistani and Saudi mediators are understood to be underway.

Although both sides previously expressed some hope of reaching an agreement, Iran's Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council on Tuesday cast doubt on progress toward a deal, calling the U.S. response to their demands "not convincing."
CBS/AFP
Iran says midterm results reflect rejection of war
Iran's chief negotiator said Wednesday the midterm election results mean Americans have rejected the war with his country.
"Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message," Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf said in a post on X.
He cited the increased cost of living or "conscience" as two of the possible reasons for the widespread Republican losses in Tuesday's vote.
"If the U.S. govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare," Ghalibaf added.
Trump acknowledges war with Iran partially to blame for GOP's election defeat
President Trump acknowledged on Tuesday night that the war with Iran was partially responsible for the Republicans' defeat in the midterm elections.
In a phone interview with Fox News, Mr. Trump said "part of it was Iran" when explaining the result of the elections, but that "at the same time, people understand the importance of what I've done."
In a separate interview with the The Wall Street Journal, the president reiterated his comments and added that he does not regret starting the war with Tehran.
"I don't think about it. I did the right thing. I would have done it again," he told the newspaper.
Qatar is said to expect feedback from U.S. and Iran on latest peace proposal within 36 hours

Qatari mediators expect feedback within 36 hours from Iranian and U.S. negotiators on new ideas aimed at getting both sides closer to a deal to end the war, Reuters reported Tuesday, citing an official briefed on the talks.
"The mediators came up with a new suggestion to move the process along, and it's currently being studied by the two sides," the official told Reuters.

Efforts to reach a deal to prevent a return to fighting between Iran and the U.S. have ramped up recently. President Trump has said he is still open to an agreement, but has also threatened to resume major U.S. strikes after Tuesday's midterm elections in the U.S.
On the eve of the elections, Mr. Trump again expressed hope that an agreement could still be reached, claiming Tehran wanted a settlement "as soon as possible."
Iranian officials declared Monday that the ball "is in the U.S. court" and they said Iran's core demands to end the war would not be altered.
